title: Additional project and data management notes
text:
1 Introduction
This page contains additional notes on project and data management: sharing data and code across projects, symbolic links, NCBI’s databases and downloading genomes and reads from NCBI, checking file integrity with checksums, file permissions, and more about file compression. (For transferring files to and from OSC, see the SSH and command-line file transfer page.)
Run the commands on this page from your personal dir, /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER, and follow the sections in order, since some of them change your working dir.

title: Additional project and data management notes
section: 2 When projects share data and/or code
text:
2 When projects share data and/or code
From Wilson et al. (2017):

As a rule of thumb, divide work into projects based on the overlap in data and code files:

If 2 research efforts share no data or code, they will probably be easiest to manage independently.
If they share more than half of their data and code, they are probably best managed together.
If you are building tools that are used in several projects, the common code should probably be in a project of its own.


To access files outside of the project (e.g., shared across projects), it is easiest to create links (i.e. shortcuts/aliases) to these files (see below for how to do this):







The data is located in project1 but used in both projects.project2 contains a link to the data.


But shared data or scripts are generally better stored in separate folders, and then linked to by each project using them:







Now, the data is in its own top-level folder, with links to it in both projects.


These strategies do decrease the portability of your project, and moving the shared files even within your own computer will cause links/shortcuts to break. A more portable method is to keep shared (multi-project) files online — this is especially feasible for scripts under version control:







A set of scripts shared by two projects is stored in an online repository like at GitHub.


For data, this is also possible but often not practical due to file sizes. It’s easier after data has been deposited in a public repository.

title: Additional project and data management notes
text:
3 Symbolic links
As shown above, a convenient way to use files that are stored outside of a project is with symbolic links (“symlinks”): small files that merely point to another file or dir, much like a shortcut (Windows) or alias (Mac).
cd sandbox

3.1 Creating symlinks
You can create a symlink with ln -s:

When you only provide the source file or or dir, it creates a link of the same name in your working dir:
ln -s /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/garrigos/data/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz
ls -l
lrwxrwxrwx 1 jelmer PAS0471 57 Nov  5 10:12 S64_R1.fastq.gz -> /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/garrigos/data/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz
You can also give a path to the link, such as simply a different name:
ln -s /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/garrigos/data/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz shared.fastq.gz
# Both the original link and the new link are now in your working dir:
ls -l
lrwxrwxrwx 1 jelmer PAS0471 57 Nov  5 10:12 S64_R1.fastq.gz -> /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/garrigos/data/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz
lrwxrwxrwx 1 jelmer PAS0471 57 Nov  5 10:12 shared.fastq.gz -> /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/garrigos/data/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz

Above, you could see that in the long-format ls output, symlinks start with an l and show their target after the ->.
Once you have a symlink, you can use it like the original file or dir. For example:
zcat shared.fastq.gz | head -n 4
TODO
You can link to a dir in the same way, or link to all files in a dir at once with a wildcard:

# Fictional examples
# Link to a dir: creates a link 'project1/scripts/shared_scripts':
ln -s /fs/ess/PAS3493/shared_scripts project1/scripts/

# Link to each of the files in a dir:
ln -s /fs/ess/PAS3493/shared_scripts/* project1/scripts/







WarningUse absolute paths for the source to be safe



Above, you may have noticed that we used the absolute path to the source file. This is not strictly necessary, but it is safer than using a relative path. If you use a relative path for the source, it is interpreted relative to the location of the link, not to your working dir. For example, running the following from your personal dir creates a broken link, because it points to sandbox/garrigos/README.md, which doesn’t exist:

ln -s garrigos/README.md sandbox/

The easiest way to avoid this is to use absolute paths for the source, e.g. with the $PWD variable, which contains your working dir:
ln -s "$PWD"/garrigos/README.md sandbox/




3.2 Removing symlinks
To remove a symlink, use rm or unlink. This only removes the link itself, not the file or dir it points to. For example, remove the two links you created above:
rm shared.fastq.gz
unlink S64_R1.fastq.gz
The original file is still there:
ls /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/garrigos/data/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz
/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/garrigos/data/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz
A symlink to a dir is a point of entry to the original dir: anything you do through the link affects the original files. To see this, create a link to your garrigos/fastq dir (the relative source path works here, because it is relative to the location of the link, sandbox):
ln -s ../garrigos/fastq fastq-link
Listing the link’s contents shows the files in the original dir:
ls fastq-link | head -n 2
S63_R1.fastq.gz
S63_R2.fastq.gz
So, rm fastq-link/*.fastq.gz would remove your original FASTQ files! To remove only the link itself, use rm without -r (the link is a file, even when it points to a dir):
rm fastq-link







WarningWatch out for trailing slashes



rm -r fastq-link only removes the link, but rm -r fastq-link/ (with a trailing slash, which tab completion may add) follows the link and removes the contents of the original dir!



 Exercise: Symbolic links

Create a symlink called pp5006 in your Home dir that points to your personal dir in the project dir (/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER). What would the link have been called if you hadn’t given it a name?
Predict what each of the following commands would remove (don’t run them!):

rm ~/pp5006
rm -r ~/pp5006/garrigos
rm -r ~/pp5006/




   Click to see the solution


Without a link name, the link gets the name of the last part of the source path, which is your username:
ln -s /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER ~/pp5006

Only the link.
Your original garrigos dir in the project dir.
Everything inside your personal dir in the project dir (the link itself remains)!

title: Additional project and data management notes
text:
4 Downloading data from NCBI
In week 11, you downloaded files with <code>wget</code> from an NCBI FTP dir. This section introduces NCBI’s databases more broadly, and shows two more convenient ways to download genomes and sequencing reads.

4.1 NCBI’s databases
The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), part of the US National Institutes of Health (NIH), hosts dozens of databases, all of which you can search from its homepage. Those you are most likely to use for omics work are:

GenBank — The archive of all publicly available DNA sequences, from single genes to entire genome assemblies. Records are submitted by researchers, and NCBI doesn’t curate them, so GenBank can contain many (near-)identical sequences and quality varies. GenBank exchanges data daily with its European (ENA) and Japanese (DDBJ) counterparts, so all three contain the same sequences.
RefSeq (“Reference Sequence”) — A curated, non-redundant set of genomes, transcripts, and proteins, derived from GenBank records and annotated by NCBI. You can recognize RefSeq records by their accession number prefixes: for example, genome assemblies start with GCF_ in RefSeq and with GCA_ in GenBank. The Culex pipiens genome you’ve worked with (GCF_016801865.2) is a RefSeq assembly.
Sequence Read Archive (SRA) — Raw reads from high-throughput sequencing. Each sequencing run has an accession number starting with SRR (or ERR or DRR when it was submitted to ENA or DDBJ, respectively), and runs are grouped into BioSamples (SAMN...) and BioProjects (PRJNA...). For example, the reads in your garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz file have headers starting with @ERR10802863, the accession number of that sample’s sequencing run.
Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) — Processed gene expression data like count tables, with links to the raw reads in the SRA.
BLAST databases — BLAST is a tool to find sequences that are similar to a query sequence. It searches databases that NCBI builds from the above, such as core_nt (nucleotide sequences) and nr (non-redundant protein sequences). You can run BLAST searches on the BLAST website, or for many sequences, with the command-line version (BLAST+) and pre-built databases that you can download from NCBI’s FTP site (note that these databases are very large).



4.2 Finding a reference genome for any species

Go to the genome part of NCBI’s datasets portal https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/.
Type in the name of a species (or other taxonomic level).







Select an appropriate taxonomic match within the search box, and press Enter. You will get a list of available genomes:







All else being equal (e.g. if it’s the right subspecies), it is generally a good idea to pick the “Reference” genome which is highlighted with a green checkmark, i.e. TS_CPP_V2 in the screenshot above. Click on the name of the desired genome, and you will see a page like this:







There are multiple ways of downloading. The FTP dir that you downloaded from in week 11 can be accessed by clicking the “FTP” button shown in the screenshot above. But you can also use the genome’s accession number (here, GCF_016801865.2) to download its files with the datasets tool, as shown next.



4.3 Downloading genomes with datasets
NCBI’s datasets command-line tool downloads genomes (and other data) by accession number or taxon name, and is especially useful when you need multiple or many genomes. It is not available as a module at OSC, so we’ll run it with a container. Run the commands in this section from your sandbox dir, where the previous section left you:
DATASETS_CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/ncbi-datasets-cli:18.39.0--018edd56cfbf78e2
apptainer exec "$DATASETS_CONTAINER" datasets --version

To download the Culex pipiens genome sequence, annotation (GFF), and protein sequences:
apptainer exec "$DATASETS_CONTAINER" datasets download genome accession GCF_016801865.2 \
    --include genome,gff3,protein --filename culex.zip
The download is a single ZIP file, which you can extract with unzip:
unzip culex.zip -d culex

# List all files (but not dirs) inside the 'culex' dir:
find culex -type f
The files are in culex/ncbi_dataset/data/GCF_016801865.2/, and unlike the files in the FTP dir, they are not gzipped.
datasets really shines when you need many genomes — for example, you can download all RefSeq reference genomes for a genus. Use datasets summary first to see how many genomes there are, since this can be a lot of data:

# [Example commands - no need to run these]
# Print info about the reference genomes for the genus Culex (in JSON format):
apptainer exec "$DATASETS_CONTAINER" datasets summary genome taxon culex --reference

# Download their genome sequences:
apptainer exec "$DATASETS_CONTAINER" datasets download genome taxon culex \
    --reference --include genome --filename culex_all.zip







TipDownloading large numbers of genomes (Click to expand)





For large downloads, use the --dehydrated option: datasets download will then only download a small ZIP file with metadata and the locations of the files. After unzipping it, datasets rehydrate --directory <dir> downloads the actual files, and you can rerun that command to resume if the download gets interrupted.





4.4 Downloading reads from the SRA
There are several ways to download FASTQ files from the SRA:

SRA explorer is a simple website where you can enter an accession number (e.g. of a BioProject) to get download links and curl commands for the FASTQ files.
The SRA Toolkit is NCBI’s official set of command-line tools, which includes prefetch and fasterq-dump.

Like datasets, the SRA Toolkit is not available as a module at OSC, so we’ll again use a container. With the SRA Toolkit, downloading the full set of reads for sample S63 of the Garrigós et al. dataset (the files in garrigos/fastq only contain a subset) takes two steps: prefetch downloads the data in NCBI’s own compressed format, and fasterq-dump converts that to FASTQ files:

# [Example commands - no need to run these]
SRATOOLS_CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/sra-tools:3.4.1--c9eb93771eedd04e

apptainer exec "$SRATOOLS_CONTAINER" prefetch ERR10802863
apptainer exec "$SRATOOLS_CONTAINER" fasterq-dump \
    --split-files --threads 4 --outdir fastq ERR10802863
gzip fastq/*.fastq


For paired-end data, --split-files produces separate files for forward and reverse reads: ERR10802863_1.fastq and ERR10802863_2.fastq.
fasterq-dump writes uncompressed FASTQ files, which you’ll want to gzip.







TipDownloads in batch jobs



Downloading reads for many samples can take a long time, so this is best done in a Slurm batch job.








NoteAlternative: installing these tools with Conda (Click to expand)





Instead of using containers, you can also install datasets and the SRA Toolkit in Conda environments. This can be especially useful for datasets, since you may want to run several commands interactively, e.g. to explore which genomes are available before deciding what to download. After activating a Conda environment, you can simply type the commands without the apptainer exec <container-URI> prefix.

# [Example commands - no need to run these]
# Create the environments (only needed once):
module load miniconda3/25.11.1-py312
conda create -y -n ncbi-datasets conda-forge::ncbi-datasets-cli
conda create -y -n sra-tools bioconda::sra-tools

# Activate an environment and run its commands:
conda activate ncbi-datasets
datasets summary genome taxon culex --reference

title: Additional project and data management notes
text:
5 Checking file integrity with checksums
When you receive FASTQ files from a sequencing facility, or download files from a public repository, they are often accompanied by a small text file with a name like md5.txt, md5checksums.txt, or sha256sums.txt.
Such a file contains so-called checksums, a sort of digital fingerprint for files, which you can use to check whether your copy of these files is completely intact (e.g., that a transfer didn’t get cut short). A checksum is a short string computed from a file’s contents, in such a way that if even one character in the file changes, the checksum will be completely different. For example, you can compute an md5 checksum with the md5sum command — here, for a string of text rather than a file:
echo "bioinformatics is fun" | md5sum
010b5ebf7e207330de0e3fb0ff17a85a  -
echo "bioinformatic is fun" | md5sum
45cc2b76c02b973494954fd664fc0456  -
(The - means that md5sum read its input from standard in rather than from a file.)

5.1 Checking a downloaded file
The NCBI FTP dir with the Culex pipiens genome files that you downloaded from in week 11 also contains a checksum file, md5checksums.txt. Download it into your garrigos/ref dir:
# Move back from 'sandbox' to your personal dir
cd ..
wget -P garrigos/ref https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/016/801/865/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2/md5checksums.txt
The file has one line per file in the FTP dir, with the checksum in the first column and the file name in the second. Let’s look up the line for the protein FASTA file that you downloaded in the w11c exercise1:
cd garrigos/ref
grep "V2_protein.faa.gz" md5checksums.txt
d593406dc180606713164a17c1a05d0a  ./GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_protein.faa.gz
Now, compute the checksum for your copy of the file:
md5sum GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_protein.faa.gz
d593406dc180606713164a17c1a05d0a  GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_protein.faa.gz
The two are identical, so your download is intact. Rather than comparing checksums by eye, you can let md5sum do the comparison with its -c (check) option. This option takes lines in the format above (from a file or from standard in), computes the checksum for each listed file, and compares it to the listed one:
grep "V2_protein.faa.gz" md5checksums.txt | md5sum -c
./GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_protein.faa.gz: OK

We only passed the line for the protein file, because md5checksums.txt lists ~190 files and we only have a few of them. When a sequencing facility sends you a checksum file for exactly your FASTQ files, you can simply run md5sum -c md5.txt.
Run the check from inside the dir with the files, because the file names in a checksum file are usually relative paths (here, ./<file-name>).

If a file doesn’t match, md5sum clearly says so, and you should download or transfer that file again:
./GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_protein.faa.gz: FAILED
md5sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match
When you’re done, move back to your personal dir:
cd ../..






NoteSHA checksums



Instead of md5 checksums, you may also encounter SHA-256 checksums. These work the same way, with the sha256sum command (e.g. sha256sum -c sha256sums.txt).



 Exercise: Checksums of an unzipped file
Say that you unzipped the genome FASTA file, so you now have GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_genomic.fna rather than ...fna.gz.

If you computed the md5 checksum of your unzipped FASTA file, would it match the one listed in md5checksums.txt for ..._genomic.fna.gz? Why (not)?
What does this imply about when you should check checksums of downloaded files?



   Click to see the solution


No: the checksum is computed from the exact contents of a file, and the unzipped file has completely different contents (bytes) than the zipped file, even though it represents the same sequences.
Check checksums right after downloading or transferring, before you modify, unzip, or rename the files.

title: Additional project and data management notes
text:
6 File permissions

6.1 Introduction to file permissions
File “permissions” are what different categories of users are permitted to do with files and dirs. Being able to view and modify file permissions is useful when you:

Want to make your data read-only to prevent accidental modification or deletion
Need to share files with other users at OSC

There are three different file permissions that can be independently controlled:

Read (r) permissions allow you to read and copy files.
Write (w) permissions allow you to modify or overwrite files.
Execute (x) permissions allow you to directly execute a file (see the box below).

For dirs, write permissions determine whether files can be added, removed, or renamed inside them. So, whether you can move or delete a file depends on the permissions of its dir, not of the file itself.
While it is possible to set permissions for individual users, they are most easily and commonly set for three different user categories:

Owner (or “user”) (u) — By default, this is the person who created the file or dir. This includes cases where this person merely copied or downloaded files: e.g., after you have copied someone else’s FASTQ files, you are the owner of these copies.
Group (g) — At OSC, the group category is at the OSC Project level.
Other (o) — Any other user.

You can also refer to all three of these categories at once with a (all).






NoteExecuting a file?



Executing a file means running it as a program/command. For example, when we run the FastQC program with the command fastqc, we are really executing a binary (executable) file somewhere on the system. Similarly, self-written shell scripts can be executed if they have execute permissions set.




6.2 Viewing file permissions
To show file permissions, use ls with the -l (long format) option that we’ve seen before, which should show you something like this:
ls -lh garrigos
total 2.5K
drwxrwx---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep  9 13:46 fastq
drwxrwx---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep  9 13:46 meta
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 2.3K Sep  9 13:46 README.md
drwxrwx---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep  9 13:46 ref
drwxrwx---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 16 13:26 sandbox
With annotations:











Important“Groups” at OSC



When you create a file in the PAS3493 project dir, all members of the OSC project PAS3493 get the “group” permissions for it. That is true even if the group displayed in the ls -l output shown above is a different one, e.g. PAS0471 for me (my personal default group at OSC). This works through so-called “access control lists” (ACLs), which is what the + at the end of the permission string indicates (to see the ACL of a file, run getfacl <file>).


Here is an overview of the file permission notation in ls -l output:





For example:

rwxrwxr-x means: read, write, and execute permissions are set for the owner (first rwx) and the group (second rwx), and read and execute but not write permissions for others (r-x at the end).
rw-rw-r-- means: read and write but not execute permissions are set for both the owner (first rw-) and the group (second rw-), and only read permissions for others (r-- at the end).







WarningDefault permissions at OSC



Most commonly, files and dirs that you create at OSC will by default have:

Read permissions for owner (you) and group
Write permissions only for owner (you)

However, this is not always the case, and I am personally sometimes vexed by file permissions at OSC. For instance, in our PAS3493 project, the default permissions appear to include write permissions for the group. I’m not certain why, but it may be because this is an “Educational” project.
More generally, by default:

OSC users that are not members of a specific project can’t access that project’s files in /fs/ess/ and /fs/scratch at all.
Other OSC users cannot access your personal Home dir files – so it’s never a good idea to keep files there that should be accessible to collaborators.




 Exercise: Viewing file permissions

Could your classmates (members of the PAS3493 group) edit the README.md file in your garrigos dir? Check with ls -l.
The -d option makes ls show info about a dir itself, rather than its contents. Run ls -ld ~ to see your Home dir’s permissions: what do these mean for your classmates’ access to any of the files in your Home dir?



   Click to see the solution


Most likely yes: if the permissions are rw-rw----, the group has write permissions.
You’ll most likely see drwx------: only you have any permissions, so nobody else can even get into your Home dir, no matter what the permissions of the files inside it are.





6.3 Changing file permissions
Let’s create a file to play around with file permissions:
# Create a test file
mkdir -p sandbox
cd sandbox
touch testfile.txt

# Check the default permissions
ls -l testfile.txt
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 0 Mar  7 13:36 testfile.txt
To change a file’s permissions, you can use the chmod command. There are two main ways to use this command, one of which uses symbols as follows:

+ : add a permission
- : remove a permission
= : set permissions to exactly this

These are used with both the kind of permission (r / w / x) and the user category (a / u / g / o). For example, a+r means that for all, you add (+) read permissions. Let’s see some commands:

To add read (r) permissions for all (a):
chmod a+r testfile.txt

ls -l testfile.txt
-rw-rw-r--+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 0 Mar  7 13:40 testfile.txt
To set read + write + execute (rwx) permissions for all (a):
chmod a=rwx testfile.txt

ls -l testfile.txt
-rwxrwxrwx+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 0 Mar  7 13:36 testfile.txt






Because the file is now “executable”, its name should display in green in your terminal.



To remove write (w) permissions for others (o):
# chmod <who>-<permission-to-remove>:
chmod o-w testfile.txt

ls -l testfile.txt
-rwxrwxr-x+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 0 Mar  7 13:36 testfile.txt








NoteAn alternative method: changing file permissions with numbers (Click to expand)





chmod alternatively accepts a series of 3 numbers (for user, group, and others, respectively) to set permissions, where each permission is “worth” the following number of points:







Nr
Permission




1
x


2
w


4
r









Nr
Permission




5
r + x


6
r + w


7
r + w + x







For example, to set read + write + execute permissions for all:
chmod 777 testfile.txt
To set read + write + execute permissions for yourself, and only read permission for the group and others:
chmod 744 testfile.txt









WarningRead/execute permissions for directories (Click to expand)





chmod is not recursive by default: you need the -R option to change permissions throughout a dir hierarchy. For example:

chmod -R g+r my-dir

One tricky and confusing aspect of file permissions is that to access anything inside a dir (e.g. cd into it or open its files), you need execute permissions for the dir! Read permissions for a dir only allow you to list the names of the files in it. This is something to take into account when you want to grant others access to your project e.g. at OSC.
To set execute permissions for everyone throughout a dir hierarchy, but only for dirs (and files that were already executable), use an X (uppercase x):

chmod -R a+X my-dir






6.4 Making your data read-only
Now, let’s see how you can make your data read-only. Here, we’ll work with the files in the garrigos/fastq/ dir, so let’s check the initial permissions first:
cd ..
ls -l garrigos/fastq/ | head -n 3
total 963552
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 21266097 Sep  9 13:46 S63_R1.fastq.gz
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 22700521 Sep  9 13:46 S63_R2.fastq.gz
To make this data read-only, you can for example run:
# Remove write permissions for all users
chmod a-w garrigos/fastq/*
After running this command, let’s check the permissions:
ls -l garrigos/fastq/ | head -n 3
total 963552
-r--r-----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 21266097 Sep  9 13:46 S63_R1.fastq.gz
-r--r-----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 22700521 Sep  9 13:46 S63_R2.fastq.gz
What happens when you try to remove a write-protected file? Let’s test this on a copy of one of the files in sandbox/, rather than on your real data, so there’s no risk of accidentally losing anything:
cp garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz sandbox/
chmod a-w sandbox/S63_R1.fastq.gz

rm sandbox/S63_R1.fastq.gz
rm: remove write-protected regular file ‘sandbox/S63_R1.fastq.gz’?
You’ll be prompted like this for every write-protected file you try to remove. Answer n (no) to keep the file for now. If you answer y (yes), the file is in fact removed: as mentioned above, removing a file is controlled by the permissions of its dir. So, read-only file permissions protect against accidentally modifying a file, but only add a confirmation prompt when removing it.






TipForce-remove with rm -f



Instead of interactively approving the removal of each write-protected file, you can also use the -f (force) option with rm.
For example, Git makes the files in its .git/objects dir read-only. So, if you would try to remove a dir with a Git repo, like garrigos, you would have to confirm the removal of many write-protected files:

rm -r garrigos/

rm: remove write-protected regular file 'garrigos/.git/objects/pack/pack-b1b2783f93b7c1f77f508f07e971dee5c0d39958.rev'? y
rm: remove write-protected regular file 'garrigos/.git/objects/pack/pack-b1b2783f93b7c1f77f508f07e971dee5c0d39958.idx'? y
rm: remove write-protected regular file 'garrigos/.git/objects/pack/pack-b1b2783f93b7c1f77f508f07e971dee5c0d39958.pack'?
Adding the -f flag will skip these prompts and remove the files directly:

rm -rf garrigos/

However, you must be careful when using the -f option to prevent accidental removal of files.


To also protect your raw data against removal, remove write permissions for the dir itself:
chmod a-w garrigos/fastq
Now, rm (even rm -f) will fail with a “Permission denied” error for any file in garrigos/fastq — unless you first add write permissions back.

 Exercise: Changing file permissions
For this exercise, you need a partner, such as a classmate who is also a member of the PAS3493 project. One person (the Owner) first creates a test file and manipulates its permissions, and the other (the Collaborator) tries to access and modify that file. After the first round, switch roles.
In each round:

The Owner creates a file in their sandbox/ dir, e.g. with echo "Hello from <your-name>" > sandbox/shared.txt, and tells the Collaborator its full path.
The Collaborator tries to read the file with cat, and to add a line to it with echo "Hi back" >> <path>.
The Owner removes write permissions for the group: chmod g-w sandbox/shared.txt.
The Collaborator first predicts what will happen when repeating step 2, and then tries it.
The Collaborator predicts whether they can remove the file with rm (answer y if prompted), and then tries it. Run ls -ld on the Owner’s sandbox dir to explain the result.



   Click to see the solution


In step 2, both commands should work, since files in our project dir are by default readable and writable for the group.
In step 4, cat still works, but adding a line fails with a “Permission denied” error.
In step 5, the removal works as long as the Owner’s sandbox dir is group-writable (drwxrwx---), because removing a file depends on the permissions of its dir, not of the file itself.

title: Additional project and data management notes
text:
7 More about file compression
This section builds on the w11c section on file compression, which covers the basics of gzip and gunzip. You’ll use a FASTA file with human chromosome 22 — download it into your sandbox dir from your personal dir:
wget -P sandbox https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg19/chromosomes/chr22.fa.gz






TipUse the du command to see the total size of a dir (Click to expand)





Given that the ls size output is not informative for dirs, how can you find out the total size of a dir and all its contents? Use the du (disk usage) command – for example:

Get the total size for a single dir:
# -h: human-readable file sizes / -s: summarize, i.e. only show the total
du -hs garrigos/fastq
941M    garrigos/fastq

Get the total size of each dir directly inside a dir, plus that of the dir itself:
# -d 1: show sizes down to a depth of 1 (= the dirs directly inside 'garrigos')
du -h -d 1 garrigos
1.0K    garrigos/meta
5.1M    garrigos/ref
941M    garrigos/fastq
946M    garrigos/.git
1.9G    garrigos




Run the commands in the box above from your personal dir, and then move into your sandbox dir:
cd sandbox

7.1 Compressing program output
Often, a program will output unzipped data to standard out, which we can immediately pipe to gzip so we only need to write the compressed file to disk (beneficial because reading/writing to files is time-consuming):

trimmer in.fastq.gz | gzip > out.fastq.gz

(Note that because the input to gzip comes from standard in, the output will by default be to standard out!)


7.2 Working with compressed data directly
Several familiar shell commands have z counterparts that work with gzipped files directly. You’ve been using zcat, the counterpart of cat, since week 4:
zcat chr22.fa.gz | head -n 4
>chr22
NNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNN
NNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNN
NNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNN
Similarly, zgrep is grep for gzipped files:
zgrep -i -n --color "AGATAGATATAT" chr22.fa.gz
589810:TATTGCAGGTAAGATGGGGCCACTCAGTACTTTAAAAAGATAGATATATA
596134:tctatctatatatagatagatatattgtagatatatctatctatatatat
966248:tatagatagatatataaaggggagtttattaagtattaactcacatgatc






NoteConcatenating compressed data





Concatenating files means you combine them into a single file, simply printing them back-to-back. When it is okay to concatenate files2, this can be done very easily.
To add a second FASTQ file to an existing gzipped file, we can simply use >>:
ls
in.fastq.gz in2.fastq
gzip -c in2.fastq >> in.fastq.gz
Even more conveniently, if we have two gzipped FASTQ files for the same sample but from different Illumina lanes:

cat smpA_L001_R1.fastq.gz smpA_L002_R1.fastq.gz > smpA_R1.fastq.gz






7.3 Archives with tar
Software, databases, and sometimes data sets are often distributed as a single .tar.gz (or .tgz) file, a so-called “tarball”. This is an “archive” file that contains multiple files and dirs, which were combined into a single file with the tar command and then gzip-compressed. Since gzip itself can only compress individual files, tar is also what you would use to pack up a dir, e.g. to share it or to back it up.

# Create (-c) a gzip-compressed (-z) archive file (-f) from the dir 'results':
tar -czvf results.tar.gz results/

# List (-t) the contents of an archive without extracting it:
tar -tzvf results.tar.gz

# Extract (-x) the contents of an archive into your working dir:
tar -xzvf results.tar.gz


The -v (verbose) option makes tar print the names of the files it processes.
The -f option should come last, because it must be directly followed by the name of the archive file.
When extracting, tar recreates the dirs stored in the archive, and overwrites existing files with the same names without asking — so when in doubt, list the contents first.


 Exercise: Compression
You have a dir with three FASTQ files: A.fastq, B.fastq, and C.fastq. Predict which files you would end up with after running each of the following commands (each starting from the same three files):

gzip *.fastq
gzip -c *.fastq > all.fastq.gz
tar -czf all.tar.gz *.fastq



   Click to see the solution


A.fastq.gz, B.fastq.gz, and C.fastq.gz: gzip compresses each file separately, and removes the originals.
The three original files, plus all.fastq.gz, which contains the reads of all three files back-to-back (see the box on concatenating compressed data above) — so you can no longer tell which reads came from which file!
The three original files, plus all.tar.gz, from which you can extract the three separate files again.

text:
Footnotes


If you didn’t do that exercise, first run: wget -P garrigos/ref https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/016/801/865/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_protein.faa.gz↩︎
 This does mean you’ll lose information about the origin of the original files.↩︎

title: Software management with Conda
text:
1 Introduction
This page introduces Conda, a software management tool that is an alternative to the containers you used in w6b. You will learn how to create Conda environments, install software in them, activate them, and manage them.

1.1 Setting up
To run the commands on this page yourself, start a VS Code session at https://ondemand.osc.edu in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER.

title: Software management with Conda
text:
2 What is Conda?
Conda can create so-called environments in which you can install one or more software packages. Compared to containers (see the comparison in w6a), Conda works especially well when you want to combine several programs in a single environment, or when you want to add programs to an existing environment later.






This makes Conda particularly handy for bioinformatics “utilities” like SeqKit, SAMtools, and BEDTools, which you will often want to use interactively (not just in scripts), and where you may want to pipe the output of one program into another. With all of them in one active environment, you can simply type samtools ... | seqkit ..., whereas with containers, every command would need its own apptainer exec ... prefix.



Conda installs programs from the same online software repositories that the Seqera containers you used in w6b were built from — recall the bioconda:: and conda-forge:: prefixes of the container search hits. So, any program with a bioconda:: or conda-forge:: hit in the Seqera search can also be installed with Conda. As you’ll learn below, installing a program with Conda:

Is quite straightforward
Is very uniform (the procedure is nearly identical for any program)
Doesn’t require administrative privileges

Under the hood, a Conda environment is “merely” a directory that includes the executable (binary) files for the program or programs in question. When you activate a Conda environment, that directory will be added to the collection of locations that the computer checks when you try to run a program by entering a command (this is called the $PATH).
Like with modules, Conda has a main command (conda) and several sub-commands (e.g. create, activate, deactivate, and install). For example, to activate an environment, you would use conda activate. But before you can do so, you need to create an environment.

title: Software management with Conda
section: 3 Creating Conda environments and installing software
text:
3 Creating Conda environments and installing software

3.1 Loading the Conda module
Before you can use Conda in any way, you always need to load OSC’s Miniconda module first:
module load miniconda3/25.11.1-py312






As of September 2026, the above version is only available on Pitzer. You should be on Pitzer now, but if/when you are on one of the other clusters, load this module instead:
module load miniconda3/24.1.2-py310





3.2 One-time Conda configuration
Before you can create your own environments, you should first do some one-time configuration1. The configuration will set the Conda “channels” (basically, software repositories) you want to use when installing programs. It will also set the relative priorities among channels, since one program may be available from multiple channels.
We can do this configuration with the config sub-command — run the following in your shell:
conda config --add channels bioconda     # Added first => lowest priority
conda config --add channels conda-forge  # Added last => highest priority
conda config --set channel_priority strict

Check whether the configuration was successfully saved:
conda config --get channels
--add channels 'bioconda'   # lowest priority
--add channels 'conda-forge'   # highest priority


3.3 Example: Creating an environment for TrimGalore
Now, you will create a Conda environment for the program TrimGalore, which can trim and filter reads in FASTQ files, but does not have a system-wide installation at OSC.
Here is a command that creates a new Conda environment and installs TrimGalore into it, all at once:
# [Don't run this - we'll modify this a bit below]
conda create -y -n trim-galore bioconda::trim-galore
Let’s break that command down:

create is the Conda sub-command to create a new environment.
When adding -y, Conda will not ask you for confirmation to install.
Following the -n option, you can specify the name you would like the environment to have: we used trim-galore. You can use whatever name you like for the environment, but a descriptive yet concise name is a good idea. For single-program environments, it makes sense to simply name it after the program.
With bioconda::trim-galore we indicate that we want to install the program trim-galore from the bioconda channel.

By default, Conda will install the latest available version of a program. If you create an entirely new environment for a program, like we’re doing here, that default will almost always apply. But if you’re installing into an environment that already contains other programs, it’s possible that due to compatibility issues, it will install a different version.
If you want to explicitly specify a version to install, add the version number after = following the package name. In that case, you may also want to include that version number in the Conda environment’s name, as in the below example, which you can run:
conda create -y -n trim-galore-2.3.0 bioconda::trim-galore=2.3.0
Retrieving notices: ...working... done
Channels:
 - conda-forge
 - bioconda
Platform: linux-64
Collecting package metadata (repodata.json): done
Solving environment: done

## Package Plan ##
# [...truncated...]
There should be a lot of output, with many packages that are being downloaded (these are all “dependencies” of TrimGalore), but if it works, you should see this before you get your prompt back:
Downloading and Extracting Packages

Preparing transaction: done
Verifying transaction: done
Executing transaction: done
#
# To activate this environment, use
#
#     $ conda activate trim-galore-2.3.0
#
# To deactivate an active environment, use
#
#     $ conda deactivate

title: Software management with Conda
section: 4 Creating environments for any available program
text:
4 Creating environments for any available program

4.1 Finding Conda installation info online
Minor variations on the conda create command above can be used to install almost any program for which a Conda package is available, which is the vast majority of open-source bioinformatics programs!
To find out whether a program is available, what the channel and package name are, and which versions exist, you can use the same Seqera Containers search you used in w6b: for example, searching for Cutadapt gives a bioconda::cutadapt hit, and its dropdown menu lists the available versions.
Then, that bioconda::cutadapt goes at the end of the conda create command:
# [Don't run this - example command]
conda create -y -n cutadapt bioconda::cutadapt
And to specify a version, add it after an =, e.g. bioconda::cutadapt=5.1.






NoteAlternative: Google and the Anaconda website (Click to expand)





Each Conda package also has a page on the Anaconda website, which is usually the top hit when you Google the program name together with “conda”, e.g. “cutadapt conda”:






Screenshot of Google search results for “conda cutadapt”.








Screenshot of the Conda page for Cutadapt.


The first of the example installation commands shown there, conda install bioconda::cutadapt, uses the install subcommand. This installs a program into the currently active Conda environment, which is usually not what you want: it’s better to give each program (or set of programs) a new, dedicated environment.
To turn this into a create-plus-install command like the ones above, simply replace install with create -y -n <env-name>:
# [Don't run this - example command]
conda create -y -n cutadapt bioconda::cutadapt
The Anaconda page also shows which version will be installed by default, and which older versions are available:

title: Software management with Conda
text:
5 Activating Conda environments
Using a Conda environment works much like using a module: you first make its programs available, and then run them as usual. But while the term “load” is used for modules, the term and command activate is used for Conda environments — it means the same thing.
You should be able to activate the TrimGalore environment you created above (using just its name; more on that below):
conda activate trim-galore-2.3.0
(trim-galore-2.3.0) [jelmer@p0085 jelmer]$






When you have an active Conda environment, its name is displayed as part of your prompt, as shown above!



With the TrimGalore environment activated, you should be able to use the program. To test this, simply run the trim_galore command (note the underscore: the command name differs from the package name) with the --help option:
trim_galore --help
 USAGE:

trim_galore [options] <filename(s)>

-h/--help               Print this help message and exits.
# [...truncated...]
Unlike module load, Conda will by default only keep a single environment active. Therefore, when you have environment A active and then activate environment B, the active environment will switch to B, and the program(s) in environment A will no longer be available.






NoteHaving multiple environments active with --stack (Click to expand)





If you want to have multiple Conda environments active at the same time, you can do so with the --stack option:

Activate the TrimGalore environment, if it isn’t already active:
conda activate trim-galore-2.3.0
“Stack” a MultiQC environment of mine:
conda activate --stack /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/conda/multiqc
Check that you can use both programs — output not shown, but both should successfully print help info:
multiqc --help

trim_galore --help










NoteDeactivating environments



To deactivate the currently active environment, run conda deactivate (no environment name needed):
conda deactivate




 Exercise: Create and activate a FastQC environment
OSC has a module for FastQC version 0.12.1. But say that you want to exactly reproduce an analysis from a paper that used FastQC version 0.11.9.

Create a Conda environment with FastQC version 0.11.9.


 Click for the solution.

module load miniconda3/25.11.1-py312
conda create -y -n fastqc-0.11.9 bioconda::fastqc=0.11.9

Activate the environment and check that you have the correct version of FastQC.


 Click for the solution.

conda activate fastqc-0.11.9
fastqc --version
FastQC v0.11.9

With the environment still active, run module load fastqc/0.12.1. Which version do you predict fastqc --version will report now? Check your prediction. (Hint: think about what both conda activate and module load do to your $PATH.)


 Click for the solution.

It will report version 0.12.1. Both conda activate and module load add a directory to the start of your $PATH, and the shell runs the first fastqc it finds there. So whichever you activated or loaded last wins. To avoid confusion like this, don’t mix modules and Conda environments that provide the same program.

title: Software management with Conda
text:
6 Managing your Conda environments

6.1 Where Conda environments are stored
You may have noticed that above, we merely gave the environment we created a name (trim-galore-2.3.0), and did not tell Conda where to put this environment. Similarly, we were able to activate the environment with just its name.
Conda puts environments in a personal default directory, which at OSC is ~/.conda/envs (see the conda env list output below). To instead put an environment in a location of your choice, use the -p (for “prefix”, i.e. path) option instead of -n — for example, to create the environment inside a project directory:
# [Don't run this]
conda create -y -p /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/my_project/software/conda/trim-galore \
    bioconda::trim-galore
When you do this, you will have to pass the path to the environment (rather than a name) when you activate it:
# [Don't run this]
conda activate /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/my_project/software/conda/trim-galore
As explained below, this is the approach I recommend for your research projects.






When you want to activate someone else’s Conda environment (this is possible as long as you have read-access to that dir!), you’ll always have to specify the full path to the environment’s directory.



To see which Conda environments you have, run conda env list:
conda env list
trim-galore-2.3.0       /users/PAS0471/jelmer/.conda/envs/trim-galore-2.3.0
To remove a Conda environment, use conda env remove:
conda env remove -n trim-galore-2.3.0






NoteMore Conda commands to manage your environments (Click to expand)






List all packages (programs) installed in an environment — due to dependencies, this can be a long list, even if you only actively installed one program:
conda list -n trim-galore-2.3.0
Export a plain-text “YAML” file that contains the instructions to recreate your currently-active environment (useful for reproducibility!)
conda env export --from-history > my_env.yml
The --from-history option only includes the packages you explicitly asked for (with their versions, if you specified them), rather than every dependency with platform-specific build details — which makes the file much more likely to work on another computer.
And you can use the following to create a Conda environment from such a YAML file:
conda env create -n my_env --file my_env.yml
Downloaded packages are cached in ~/.conda/pkgs, even for environments you created elsewhere with -p. This cache can grow large, so if you’re running low on space in your Home directory, clear it with:
conda clean --all






6.2 Project-specific environments
There are a number of ways to organize your Conda environments, but I recommend that you create Conda environments that are specific to a research project, rather than reusing environments across projects. That way, each project has its own record of exactly which software (and which versions) it used, and updating or breaking an environment for one project can’t affect your other projects. This does have the downside of requiring more disk space and time to set up each project, but it provides better reproducibility and maintainability.
Within a project, there are two reasonable ways to organize your environments:

A single environment for the project

You just need to activate that one environment when you’re working on your project.
The project’s software setup is described by a single environment (and can be exported to a single YAML file).
But the more programs you install into one environment, the higher the risk of running into problems due to mutually incompatible software and complicated dependency situations. Therefore, this works best for projects that only use a handful of programs.

Multiple environments for the project, e.g. one for each program or for each analysis step

Less risk of dependency problems, and each environment is quick to create.
You can update or replace one program without touching the others.
But you need to activate the right environment at each step, e.g. in each of your scripts.








What is not recommended is simply installing all programs across all your projects into one single environment. Even though this might seem easier, it doesn’t benefit reproducibility, and your environment is likely to stop functioning sooner or later.




Put your environments inside your project directory
To make your environments project-specific, create them inside your project directory with -p — for example, in a software/conda subdirectory with one or more environments, as in the example above. This has several advantages:

It is always clear which environments belong to which project, and your scripts can refer to them with the path to the environment.
Other members of your group who have access to the project directory can use the same environments.
You avoid filling up your Home directory: Conda environments consist of many small files, and Home has a limit of 1 million files (as well as 500 GB of space).
When you archive or remove a project, its software goes along with it.







NoteUsing Conda environments in shell scripts





Once you start writing shell scripts (week 7) and Slurm batch jobs (week 10), don’t rely on whatever module or environment happens to be active in your shell when you run the script. Instead, include both steps inside the script itself, so the script is self-contained and reproducible:
module load miniconda3/25.11.1-py312
conda activate /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/my_project/software/conda/trim-galore
If this gives an error like CondaError: Run 'conda init' before 'conda activate', use source activate <env> instead of conda activate <env>.





 Exercise: A project environment with two programs
FastQC and MultiQC are often used together. Following the recommendation above, create a single Conda environment with both programs, inside a software/conda subdirectory of your personal directory in the course project, /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER. Call the environment qc.

Create the environment. You can install multiple programs in one go by listing them one after the other.


 Click for the solution.

module load miniconda3/25.11.1-py312
conda create -y -p /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/software/conda/qc \
    bioconda::fastqc bioconda::multiqc

Activate the environment and check that both programs work.


 Click for the solution.

conda activate /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/software/conda/qc
fastqc --version
multiqc --version

Run conda list and look for the packages openjdk and python. You didn’t ask for either of them, so why were they installed?


 Click for the solution.

They are dependencies: FastQC is written in Java (openjdk provides Java), and MultiQC is written in Python. Conda automatically installs everything a program needs to run — which is also why environments can contain many more packages than you explicitly installed.

title: Ungraded Assignment: Set up Positron for R at OSC
text:
Introduction

Overview
By Sunday, November 8th (before our first R class), you should have Positron installed on your computer and be able to use it with R and its AI assistant at OSC.






If you run into problems with any of these steps, contact Jelmer — don’t wait until the weekend!





Why Positron?
For the R part of the course, we’ll use Positron, an IDE (Integrated Development Environment) for R and Python made by Posit, the company behind RStudio:

It has the panes you may know from RStudio, like a Console, Environment, and Plots, but it is built on VS Code, so much of it will look familiar.
Its AI assistant, Posit Assistant, can be used with your OSU API key from weeks 8 and 9. It can even see the objects in your R session, such as data frames. (RStudio Server at OSC has no AI assistant.)
Positron is the main focus of Posit’s development moving forward.

Unlike VS Code, Positron can’t be used through OnDemand at OSC. Instead, you’ll install it on your own computer and connect it to an OSC compute node, using the same setup as for a local VS Code installation.

The Extensions icon

title: Ungraded Assignment: Set up Positron for R at OSC
text:
Connect Positron to OSC

The SSH connection
Because Positron is built on VS Code, it uses the same SSH configuration as VS Code.

If you already set up a local VS Code installation at OSC with the osc-pitzer-compute connection, you don’t need to repeat that: it will automatically work in Positron too. Just do step 1 under Connect below.
If you haven’t, follow the steps in Set up the OSC connections on that page, but do them in Positron instead of VS Code — they are identical. (You don’t need to install VS Code or the Remote Development extension: Positron has this functionality built in.)



Connect

In Positron’s Settings (cog wheel  > Settings), search for remote.SSH.connectTimeout and set it to 300 (seconds), if you haven’t already.
Open the Command Palette (Ctrl/⌘+Shift+P), start typing “SSH connect”, select Remote-SSH: Connect to Host..., and then select osc-pitzer-compute.
A new Positron window will open and connect to OSC. This may take 30 seconds or more while a compute job is starting. If you’re asked whether you “trust the authors”, click Trust and Continue.
Open your personal folder: in the Explorer, click Open Folder and enter /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>, where <user> is your OSC username.












Like in VS Code, this folder will now appear in Positron’s “Recent” list on the Welcome page, so next time you can reconnect with a single click.





Make R available
R is installed at OSC, but has to be loaded as a module (as you learned in week 6). To make sure Positron finds R, you’ll load the module in your shell settings file ~/.bashrc:

Open a terminal in Positron (Terminal > New Terminal) and run:
echo 'module load gcc/12.3.0 R/4.5.2' >> ~/.bashrc
Reload Positron: in the Command Palette, start typing “Reload Window”, and select “Developer: Reload Window”.
Positron should now start R in the Console in the bottom panel.






WarningIf you’re seeing a Python console instead of R (Click to expand)






In the top-right corner of the Positron window, you’ll see something like this:





Click on the Python indicator, and then select New Console Session:





Select the R version:





The top-right corner should now show R, and your console should have switched to R as well:
















NoteWhy ~/.bashrc? (Click to expand)





Commands in ~/.bashrc are run every time you start a new shell at OSC (see the shell configuration self-study page). This is not a permanent solution: the R versions available at OSC change over time, so you may need to update this line in the future.





Install Posit Assistant at OSC
Extensions like Posit Assistant need to be installed separately on the remote: open the Extensions view, find Posit Assistant, and click “Install in SSH: osc-pitzer-compute”.





Your settings from earlier (API key and model) will carry over.

Test it

In the R Console, create a small data frame:
df <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = rnorm(10))
In the Posit Assistant panel, ask:

Create a scatter plot of x vs y from df

Posit Assistant should write code for a plot and ask for permission to run it: click Allow.





It produces the plot, and shows it in its own panel along with suggestions for next steps. The plot should also appear in the Plots pane, since it was made by R code that ran in your R session at OSC.












Note that you didn’t have to tell Posit Assistant what df contains: it can see the objects in your R session.

title: Graded Assignment 4:Shell scripts with and without genAI
text:
Overview and grading

What you’ll practice
In this graded assignment, you will first do the following without genAI: write a shell script to run the program TrimGalore, run it, and interpret its output. Then, you’ll use Claude Code to review and extend your script, to write a loop that runs it for multiple samples, and to summarize the results.


Submission expectations

Deadline: Sunday Oct 25th at 11:59 pm.
Submission: Like for GA3, you will submit your assignment by tagging the instructors in an Issue in your GitHub repository, as per the last step below.







NoteOral examination



As explained in GA3, each of you will have one short oral examination, for one of GA3, GA4, or GA5. If you already had yours for GA3, you won’t have another one. If not, it may be for this assignment, in which case you should also be able to explain any code that genAI wrote for you.




Academic integrity












Use of generative AI tools is permitted, except in Part B (see below).



Open-book research for the assignment is permitted.



Getting help on the assignment is not permitted.



Collaborating, or completing the assignment with others, is not permitted.



Copying or reusing previous work is not permitted.



APA Citations and/or formatting for this assignment are not required.













NoteGenAI expectations



This is the first assignment in which you are allowed to use generative AI. The general guidelines from now on are:

You can use genAI as long as you can explain what your code does. If genAI produces commands or constructs not covered in class, do the research needed to understand them.
Whatever the source, you remain responsible for whether the code is correct.

That said, this assignment has two exceptions to these guidelines:

You must do Part B without genAI assistance (same rules as GA1–GA3). This is because in Part C, you’ll compare genAI output with a script and answers you produced yourself.
In Part C, genAI use is not just allowed but required: you must use Claude Code specifically (not another genAI tool), and document how you used it (item 17).





Rubric
You can earn a maximum of 0.5 points for each of the 20 numbered questions/items below (you’ll get 0.25 points for partially correct answers, and 0 points for missing or incorrect answers).

title: Graded Assignment 4:Shell scripts with and without genAI
text:
Detailed steps






NoteUpdate (Oct 23): Sonnet 5.5 now works — switch to it if you want (Click to expand)





The newer (and better) Sonnet 5.5 model now works with OSU’s API. You can switch to it by changing the following line in your ~/.claude/settings.json file:


~/.claude/settings.json

"ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "claude-sonnet-5",

to:


~/.claude/settings.json

"ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "claude-sonnet-5-5",

Then, start a new Claude conversation for the change to take effect. If you do this, the instructions below that mention Sonnet 5 refer to Sonnet 5.5 for you.




General

Like before, we provide a template README.md (see “Setting up” below) with a section for each question, where you can add your answers:

Add the commands you ran only where the template has a bash code block for them.
Include a command’s output only where the template has an output block for it.

For any shell script you write, follow the practices from class: start with the shebang and safe-settings lines, followed by a comment block with the script’s purpose and a usage line (as introduced in w9a), and copy any placeholder variables like $1 to descriptively named variables.
Commit your files to your Git repo as you go along, using informative commit messages. Besides the specific commits that questions ask for, commit at least once per Part.



Setting up

Start a VS Code session at OSC OnDemand as per usual, and open a terminal in that session.
Create a new dir for this assignment, /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/GA4. Then, open this dir as your VS Code folder with File > Open Folder. This will be your working dir for the entire assignment, and Claude’s workspace in Part C.
Copy the template file for this assignment, /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA4/GA4_template.md, into your working dir as README.md. You’ll use this file throughout the assignment to add your answers.



Part A: Your project dir and Git repo

Inside dir GA4, create subdirs scripts and results/fastqc. Then:

Copy the CLAUDE.md file you created in class into your working dir (Claude will use this in Part C).
Copy a FastQC report from week 7 (you’ll compare this to a later FastQC report in Part B):
cp ../week07/results/fastqc/S63_R1_fastqc.html results/fastqc/



 Help! I don’t have one or both of the files.

You can copy the CLAUDE.md file from the share dir like so:
cp /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA4/CLAUDE.md .
And the FastQC report from the share dir like so:
cp /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA3/results/fastqc/S63_R1_fastqc.html results/fastqc/

Initialize a Git repository, and create a .gitignore file that makes Git ignore the results dir. Then, commit your README.md, CLAUDE.md, and .gitignore files.



Part B: A TrimGalore script — without genAI
TrimGalore (Krueger 2026) is a commonly used tool to preprocess the reads in FASTQ files before further analysis. It’s the next step in the RNA-seq analysis workflow we’re gradually applying to the Garrigós et al. (2025) data in this course:






TrimGalore takes FASTQ files as input, and outputs filtered FASTQ files, along the way removing:

Any adapter sequences that are present in the reads1
Poor-quality bases at the end of the reads
Reads that have become very short after the prior two steps

Unlike FastQC, TrimGalore isn’t run on one FASTQ file at a time: when you have paired-end reads, like we do with the Garrigós et al. (2025) data, a single TrimGalore run should include both the R1 (forward read) and R2 (reverse read) file for one sample. This is because R1 and R2 files should remain “synced”: generally, you can’t remove a read from an R1 file without also removing its mate from the R2 file.






NoteMore about TrimGalore and similar programs (Click to expand)





Several largely equivalent tools exist for this kind of FASTQ preprocessing — Trimmomatic and fastp are two other commonly used ones. TrimGalore started out as a “wrapper” around yet another tool called Cutadapt, but since version 2 (which we’re using), it is a standalone program. Two advantages of TrimGalore are:

It will auto-detect the adapters that are present in your reads.
It can automatically run FastQC on the trimmed sequences.





Get a link from the Seqera Containers website to a container with TrimGalore version 2.3.0 (note: the package is called trim-galore). Then, print TrimGalore’s help info by running trim_galore --help with your container link. Use this help info to find the TrimGalore options to:

Tell it that your reads are paired-end2
Set the output dir
Make it run FastQC on the trimmed FASTQ files

Also use the help info to find the default thresholds for A) the base quality score and B) the read length, and report what they are. (You don’t have to change these thresholds, the defaults work fine for us.)
Write a shell script scripts/trimgalore.sh that runs TrimGalore on the R1 and R2 FASTQ files of one sample:

The script should accept three arguments: the R1 FASTQ file, the R2 FASTQ file, and the output dir.
Use the three options from question 3.
Include “logging statements” with echo, like in the FastQC script from class. (You don’t need to separately print the TrimGalore version, since it is printed automatically when you run the program.)







WarningStick to using the default setting for the number of cores, for now. (Click to expand)





Since you’re running the program interactively on your single-core VS Code compute job, you only have 1 core at your disposal. Using 1 core is TrimGalore’s default, so don’t adjust this setting here with TrimGalore’s --cores option. Next week, you’ll learn to submit scripts as batch jobs, which gives you the opportunity to use multiple cores to speed things up.



Run your script for the FASTQ files of sample S63 (in ../garrigos/fastq), with results/trimgalore as the output dir. Then, list the files in the output dir, and briefly describe what each type of output file contains. Once your script works, commit it. (If it failed, try to fix your script, and briefly describe the problem and your fix in the README.)
TrimGalore printed quite a bit of logging output to the screen, while additional information is saved in the *_trimming_report.txt output files. Use this information to answer the following:

Which adapter sequence did TrimGalore look for in the reads, and how did it decide on this (you didn’t tell it which adapter to look for)?
In each file (R1 and R2), in what percentage of reads were adapters detected?
In each file, were more bases removed as a result of quality trimming or adapter trimming?
What percentage of read pairs were removed altogether?

TrimGalore also reports on poly-G trimming. Newer Illumina sequencers, such as the NextSeq and NovaSeq, use a “two-color” chemistry in which G bases produce no signal. As a result, when the signal is lost near the end of a read, the sequencer calls a stretch of false Gs, which should be trimmed off. Use TrimGalore’s logging output and the trimming reports to answer the following:

Did TrimGalore do poly-G trimming, and did you have to tell it to?
What does TrimGalore conclude about the sequencing technology that was used to generate these reads?
Was more poly-G trimming done in the R1 or the R2 file? (Optional: any idea why?)

Compare TrimGalore’s FastQC report for the trimmed R1 file with the FastQC report for the raw R1 file of the same sample (the one you copied to results/fastqc).

Name at least two differences between the reports. Do things look better now in terms of pass/warn/fail status?
Do the short reads with only Ns, which you saw in week 4, appear to have been removed? If so, was that due to the length threshold, or something else?
Name something you didn’t expect or are confused about.



 To see the two files side by side, download one or both (Click to expand)

The HTML preview in VS Code won’t let you preview each file in a separate tab. So, to view them side by side, you can download one or both of the FastQC reports: in the file explorer, right-click on a file and click “Download…”. Then, open the downloaded file(s) in your browser.




Part C: Bring in genAI
Now that you have a script that you wrote yourself and that you know works, you’ll use Claude Code to review and extend it. Some general guidelines:

Use the Claude extension in VS Code, with:

The permission mode set to Manual throughout
The default model and effort level (Sonnet 5 Medium), except where a question explicitly asks you to change them

Start a new conversation for each question, to keep the context window small (and to save costs).
For questions 10, 11, 13, and 14, export the conversation when you’re done with it, using the /export command as shown in class. Save it in a dir doc/ai in your working dir, with a file name that includes the question number, like q10_review-sonnet.txt. (These are the conversations that produced code you kept, or that informed your decisions. For the other questions, your notes in the README are enough.)
For each question, record in your README what you asked, what you got, and what you concluded after checking it.
In this specific case, you are graded on your evaluation of Claude’s output, not on whether Claude happened to give a good answer. A well-documented case in which you caught Claude being wrong is worth full points.


With your scripts/trimgalore.sh open in the editor, and the Claude panel open, check that the script is added as context (you should see its name below the prompt box). Then, using the default model and effort level (Sonnet 5 Medium), ask Claude to review your script, for example:

Review this shell script. List the 5 most important problems or improvements, most important first, with a one-sentence reason for each. Don’t change it yet.

In your README, briefly list Claude’s suggestions, and for each, say whether and why you agree with it, disagree with it, or don’t understand it. Did it suggest anything that you think is wrong, or that conflicts with how we’ve been writing scripts in this course? Did it refer to any of the conventions in your CLAUDE.md?
Finally, type /usage in the prompt box, and add the estimated cost of this conversation to your README.


 Some hints about possible feedback (Click to expand)


If you use “# Copy the placeholder variables” as a comment, Claude is likely to comment on that, calling it confusing or inaccurate. This is technically fair, but rather nitpicky, and you can ignore it.


Now, get a second review from an even more capable model. Start a new conversation, so that this model doesn’t see the first review. Then, switch the model to Opus 5.5 with effort level High. Give it the exact same prompt as in the previous question. If Opus asks permission to run a command that only prints information, such as TrimGalore’s help info, you can allow it. When it’s done, type /usage again, and add the estimated cost of this conversation to your README.
You don’t need to evaluate each of Opus’s suggestions separately. Instead, compare the two reviews:

Which suggestions did only one of the two models make?
Did either model claim something that you know is wrong, for example based on your successful run in question 6?
Did either model check its claims, for example by running commands?
Did Opus’s review change your mind about any of your answers to question 10?
How did the costs of the two reviews compare?
Which review would you trust more, and why? Was the difference worth the difference in cost?

The output of genAI models varies between runs, so there is no single “correct” outcome of this comparison. When you’re done, switch back to Sonnet 5 Medium for the remaining questions.
Both reviews probably suggested checking that the input FASTQ files exist (if not, you’ll make this change anyway in the next question). Before making any changes, run your script with an R1 FASTQ file path that doesn’t exist. What happens, and at which point does the script stop?
Now, ask Claude to implement this suggestion, for example:

In scripts/trimgalore.sh, add a check that both input FASTQ files exist, and exit with an informative error message if they don’t.

Claude will show you the proposed change as a diff: read it before you accept it.
It may also ask permission to create a diary file, as per your CLAUDE.md: if so, allow that too.
Then, test the updated script with the same non-existent file name as in the previous question. Does it behave the way Claude claimed it would? And given what you saw before the change, how useful is this check?
Finally, commit the updated script. Your Git history now shows exactly what Claude changed in your script.
Ask Claude to write a for loop that runs your script for multiple samples, for example:

Write a for loop that runs scripts/trimgalore.sh for the 7 samples whose IDs start with S6, with output dir results/trimgalore. I will run the loop from the GA4 dir. Only show me the loop: don’t add it to a file, and don’t run it.

Add the loop to your README, but don’t run it yet (you will do so in the next question). Review the w7b self-study section, and think about whether this loop will:

Run the script once per sample, rather than once per FASTQ file?
Get the correct R2 file for each R1 file? If you don’t understand how it does this, ask Claude to explain that part.
Only run for the 7 samples whose IDs start with S6 (S63 to S69)?

If you ended up changing the loop because of concerns with the above points, explain what you changed and why.
Test the loop by putting echo before the bash command, so that it only prints the commands it would run. If those look right, remove the echo and run the loop for real (this will take about 2 minutes). If you get any errors, fix them with help from Claude. When it’s done, check the output files in results/trimgalore: are all 7 samples represented?
Ask Claude for a command that summarizes your TrimGalore results: for each sample, the percentage of read pairs that were removed. For example:

Give me a simple command that prints, for each sample, the percentage of read pairs that TrimGalore removed, based on the output files in results/trimgalore. I’m a shell beginner, so only use basic commands like grep, cut, and for loops.

Run the command, and verify its output:

If the output doesn’t look right, ask Claude to explain how it works and/or to fix it.
Does the value for S63 match your answer to question 7?
In your own words, how does the command work? If it uses anything we didn’t cover in class, ask Claude to explain it.

Document your genAI use: check that your doc/ai dir contains the exported conversations for questions 10, 11, 13, and 14. If you forgot one, reopen that conversation from Claude’s list of past conversations, and export it then. Then, commit the doc/ai dir to your Git repo.
Based on your experiences in this part, add one or more instructions to your CLAUDE.md that would have improved Claude’s output (for example, to prevent a suggestion you disagreed with in question 10 or 11). If you really can’t think of anything along these lines, you can instead add an instruction that you simply think would be interesting to try. Then, start a new conversation and test whether Claude follows the new instruction. In your README, describe what you added and what happened, and commit your updated CLAUDE.md.
Write a short reflection in your README (one or two paragraphs) about your experience with Claude in this assignment. Any thoughtful reflection will earn full points, but here are some example questions you can answer if you like:

What did you find most helpful about using Claude?
What challenges did you encounter?
Did Claude tell you anything that turned out to be wrong, and how did you find out?
Were its explanations clear, or did you have to do additional research to understand them?




Part D: Publish your repo on GitHub
Finally, you’ll publish your Git repo on GitHub and submit your assignment by creating an Issue.

Make sure you have committed your final README.md. Then, create a new, empty, public repository on GitHub (e.g., named “GA4” or “PLNTPTH5006-GA4”), connect it to your local repo, and push your local repo to GitHub.
On the GitHub page for your repo, create a new Issue. Use whatever title you like, and in the text box (not the title), tag the instructors: GitHub users kstarr791 and jelmerp (using the @ notation like @kstarr791), asking them to take a look at your assignment.
