section: Exercise 4: A SeqKit batch job script with Claude
text:
Exercise 4: A SeqKit batch job script with Claude
SeqKit is a toolkit for FASTA and FASTQ files. Its seqkit stats command reports, for each input file, the number of reads, the total number of bases, and the read lengths. You’ll have Claude write a script that runs seqkit stats on all FASTQ files in a dir as a single batch job, and then check that script carefully.

If you haven’t done so already, make sure you have an updated CLAUDE.md in your week10 dir (see w10b here).
In a new Claude conversation, with the permission mode set to Manual, ask Claude to write the script, for example:

Write a script scripts/seqkit_stats.sh that runs seqkit stats on all FASTQ files in an input dir, using 4 cores, and writes the results to a TSV file in an output dir. The input dir and output dir should be arguments. Don’t run it.

Check the script and get a container link before running it:

Does it follow the conventions in your CLAUDE.md, including the #SBATCH lines?
Does the number of threads that SeqKit is told to use match --cpus-per-task?
How did it deal with SeqKit: did it want to use a container, and if so how? Regardless, you will need to obtain a container link from the Seqera Containers website yourself, and put it in the script.
Did Claude add any other #SBATCH options or lines you don’t recognize? If so, find out what they do.

It’s possible that Claude explicitly asked you to find a container link, which is the best outcome. But to make sure that it consistently does that in the future, add a line to the “Shell script conventions” section of your CLAUDE.md:


CLAUDE.md (excerpt)

- Never write container links (`oras://` URLs) yourself:
  if a script needs one, add a placeholder and ask me for the link

Add a “Step 3: Read statistics with SeqKit” section to your protocol.md, with a description and the code to submit the script for your FASTQ dir. Submit the job from your protocol, and check that it succeeded. Do the read counts in the output file make sense?

title: Week 10 exercises: Slurm batch jobs and workflows
section: Bonus: Rename the output FASTQ files
text:
Bonus: Rename the output FASTQ files
The TrimGalore output FASTQ files are oddly named, ending in _R1_val_1.fq.gz and _R2_val_2.fq.gz. This is not necessarily a problem, but could trip you up in a later step. For example, the STAR loop in the lecture’s protocol looks for trimmed files ending in _R1.fastq.gz, which is why the TrimGalore script in that protocol renames its output files.

Modify your TrimGalore script to rename the output FASTQ files after running TrimGalore, giving them the same names as the input files. Then, resubmit the script for sample S63 to check that your changes work, using a separate output dir like results/trimgalore_test.



 Hints (Click to expand)

To rename the files, you first need to extract and store the part of the file name that is basically a sample ID: the part before _R1.fastq.gz/_R2.fastq.gz. To do that, you will need to use “command substitution” and the basename command. Those are explained on the optional advanced shell scripting self-study page starting here, but we did not cover them together in class.
Here is a skeleton of the code to extract that part of the file name:
# Replace " ... " with your code.
sample_id=$( ... )
Based on that ID, you can build up the names of the TrimGalore output files and those of the desired final file names. For example:
# The name of the initial ('init') TrimGalore R1 output file will be:
R1_out_init="$outdir"/"$sample_id"_R1_val_1.fq.gz
See also this section on renaming files with loops, though realize that this situation is different, because you will do the renaming inside the script without a loop.

title: Week 10 exercises: Slurm batch jobs and workflows
text:
Solutions

Exercise 1


1. Add #SBATCH lines

The first few lines of your script should look like this:


scripts/trimgalore.sh (excerpt)

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=PAS3493
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --time=30
#SBATCH --output=slurm-trimgalore-%j.out
#SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL
set -euo pipefail


The #SBATCH lines should come right after the shebang line, and before any other code: Slurm stops reading #SBATCH lines at the first line of code.
The order of the #SBATCH lines doesn’t matter.




2. Let TrimGalore use 8 cores

Print the help info (only relevant output lines shown below):
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/trim-galore:2.3.0--a56e49e832976df4 \
    trim_galore --help
  -j, --cores <CORES>
          Number of worker threads for parallel processing (default: 1).
          At --cores 1 the worker-pool is bypassed (single thread, ~5 MB RAM).
          From --cores 2 upward, an N+4 thread model applies: N workers +
          2 decompressors + 1 batcher + 1 writer.
          Wall-clock speedup is near-linear up to --cores 8 for paired-end runs;
          beyond that, gzip-output I/O on the storage layer typically becomes
          binding before workers run out of useful per-read work,
          so additional cores help progressively less
The option is -j/--cores. Unlike FastQC’s --threads option, which only parallelizes the processing of multiple files, TrimGalore can also use multiple cores to process a single pair of files faster. So, edit the trim_galore command as follows:
apptainer exec "$TRIMGALORE_CONTAINER" \
    trim_galore \
    --cores 8 \
    --paired \
    --fastqc \
    --output_dir "$outdir" \
    "$fastq_r1" \
    "$fastq_r2"
Reserving 16 cores would probably not be worth it: according to the help info, the speedup is near-linear up to 8 cores, but beyond that, additional cores help “progressively less”. So, the job would be less than twice as fast, while your project would be billed for twice as many cores.
You may also notice that with --cores 8, TrimGalore runs 4 additional “helper” threads, e.g. to read and write the FASTQ files. That’s fine: Slurm restricts your job to the 8 reserved cores, so these threads simply share them, and setting --cores to the number of reserved cores remains a good rule of thumb.
Finally, keep in mind that our practice FASTQ files are so small that the job will be quick either way, so you may not notice much of a speedup compared to your 1-core runs in GA4. With full-size FASTQ files, multiple cores make a much bigger difference.

## Step 2: Read trimming with TrimGalore

The `trimgalore.sh` script runs TrimGalore on the paired-end FASTQ files of 1 sample at a time,
and takes 3 arguments: the R1 FASTQ file, the R2 FASTQ file, and the output dir.

```bash
for fastq_r1 in "$fastq_dir"/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    fastq_r2="${fastq_r1/_R1/_R2}"
    sbatch scripts/trimgalore.sh "$fastq_r1" "$fastq_r2" results/trimgalore
```

10. A failed TrimGalore job and the STAR step

The STAR loop would simply skip the failed sample, because its trimmed FASTQ files don’t exist. You wouldn’t get any error: all STAR jobs would succeed, and you’d just end up with one sample fewer in your count table.
You may not notice this until much later. This is why you should check that all jobs of a step succeeded before moving on, e.g. by counting the output files like you did in Exercise 2.



11. Which steps to rerun after a failed TrimGalore job?

You’d need to rerun TrimGalore and the steps that use its output, STAR and Salmon, but only for the failed sample. FastQC and MultiQC use the raw FASTQ files, so they are not affected.
You shouldn’t simply rerun the protocol’s loops, because those would submit jobs for all samples again. Instead, submit single jobs for the failed sample, e.g. for sample S63:
sbatch scripts/trimgalore.sh \
    "$fastq_dir"/S63_R1.fastq.gz "$fastq_dir"/S63_R2.fastq.gz results/trimgalore
And once that job has finished, do the same for the STAR step, and then for the Salmon step. This is one advantage of scripts that process a single sample: you can easily rerun just the part of the workflow that failed.

THREADS=4

# Initial logging

# The glob (*.fastq.gz) expands to all gzipped FASTQ files in the input dir

The value of --threads should match --cpus-per-task. (If Claude left out --threads, SeqKit would still use 4 threads, its default, but it’s better to be explicit, as your CLAUDE.md asks.)

title: Slurm batch jobs – part I
text:
1 Introduction

1.1 Learning goals

This week
As mentioned in week 7, when you learned about shell scripts:

The strategy you’ve learned so far, and that we will stick to, is writing scripts that run a single program a single time. We do this even though you commonly need to run a CLI tool many times, e.g. separately for each file or sample. That’s because at OSC and other HPC systems, you can save a lot of time by submitting a separate batch job for each file or sample, since these jobs can all run simultaneously.

This week, we’ll cover how you can submit your shell scripts as batch jobs.


This session

Different ways to start “compute jobs”: via OnDemand, with interactive jobs, and with Slurm batch jobs
How to submit scripts as batch jobs with sbatch, and where their output goes
How to specify sbatch options on the command line and inside scripts
How to monitor and cancel batch jobs with squeue and scancel




1.2 Getting ready

At https://ondemand.osc.edu, start a VS Code session in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER.
Create a week10 dir and navigate there in the terminal.
Create a scripts dir within week10.
We’ll re-use two scripts from week 7, but to make sure we all have the same scripts, copy them from a shared dir:
# You should be in week10/ now
cp -v /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/scripts/fastqc.sh scripts/
cp -v /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/scripts/printname.sh scripts/
'/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/scripts/fastqc.sh' -> 'scripts/fastqc.sh'
'/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/scripts/printname.sh' -> 'scripts/printname.sh'


 Click here to find the contents of these two scripts



scripts/printname.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

first_name="$1"
last_name="$2"

echo "First name: $first_name, last name: $last_name"




scripts/fastqc.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Script to run FastQC on a single FASTQ file
# Usage: fastqc.sh <fastq file> <outdir>

# FastQC container
CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960

# Copy the placeholder variables
fastq="$1"
outdir="$2"

# Initial logging
echo "Starting script fastqc.sh"
date
echo "Input FASTQ file:   $fastq"
echo "Output dir:         $outdir"
echo

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p "$outdir"

# Run FastQC with its container
apptainer exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --outdir "$outdir" "$fastq"

# Final logging
echo
echo "Used FastQC version:"
apptainer exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --version
echo
echo "Successfully finished script fastqc.sh"
date

title: Slurm batch jobs – part I
text:
2 Compute jobs overview
Automated scheduling software allows hundreds of people with different requirements to effectively and fairly access compute nodes at supercomputers. OSC uses Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) for this.
As you’ve learned, a reservation of resources on compute nodes is called a compute job. Here are the main ways to start a compute job at OSC:

“Interactive Apps” — Run programs with GUIs (e.g. VS Code or RStudio) in your browser through OnDemand.
Interactive shell jobs — Start an interactive shell on a compute node.
Batch (non-interactive) jobs — Run a script on a compute node “remotely”: without going to that node yourself.

We’ve already worked a lot with the VS Code Interactive App, and interactive shell jobs are covered in this week’s optional self-study material (you should rarely need these). What we’ll focus on in this session are batch jobs.

title: Slurm batch jobs – part I
text:
3 Basics of Slurm batch jobs
When you submit a batch job, you ask the Slurm scheduler to run a script “out of sight” on a compute node. While that script runs on a compute node, you will stay in your current shell at your current node. After you submit a batch job, it will continue to run even if you log off from OSC and shut down your computer.

3.1 The sbatch command
You can use Slurm’s sbatch command to submit a batch job. But first, let’s recall how we’ve run shell scripts so far:
bash scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe
First name: Jane, last name: Doe
The above command ran the script on whatever node you are on, and printed output to the screen. To instead submit the script to the Slurm queue, start by simply replacing bash with sbatch:
sbatch scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe
sbatch: error: ERROR: Job invalid: Must specify account for job
sbatch: error: Batch job submission failed: Unspecified error
However, as the error message above (“Must specify account for job”) informs us, you need to indicate which OSC Project (or as Slurm puts it, “account”) you want to use for this compute job. Use the --account= option to do this:
sbatch --account=PAS3493 scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe
Submitted batch job 56603792

This output line means your job was successfully submitted (no further job output will be printed to your screen).
The number in this output is the job ID: a unique identifier among all compute jobs by all users at OSC, which you can use to monitor and manage the job. Each of us will therefore see a different job ID pop up.
After submitting a batch job, you immediately get your prompt back. The job will run outside of your view, and you can continue doing other things in the shell while it does, or even log off. This behavior allows you to submit many jobs at the same time: you don’t have to wait for other jobs to finish, or even to start!
Note the new option style in --account=PAS3493: the option and its value are separated by an = rather than a space. Many commands accept this style for long options (those starting with --), and it’s the usual style for sbatch options.


sbatch options and script arguments
As was implicit in the command above, we can use sbatch options and script arguments in one command like so:

sbatch [sbatch-options] myscript.sh [script-arguments]

Depending on the details of the script itself, any combination of sbatch options and script arguments is possible:

# No options/arguments for either:
sbatch scripts/printname.sh

# Script arguments but no sbatch option:
sbatch scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe

# sbatch option but no script arguments:
sbatch --account=PAS3493 scripts/printname.sh

# Both sbatch option and script arguments:
sbatch --account=PAS3493 scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe




 Exercise 1: Option order
What do you think would happen if you ran the following command?
sbatch scripts/printname.sh --account=PAS3493 Jane Doe

The job is submitted and runs fine, just like when --account comes before the script name.
sbatch fails with the “Must specify account for job” error.
The job is submitted, but it prints “First name: --account=PAS3493, last name: Jane”.



 Click for the solution

B is correct. Everything after the script name is passed to the script as an argument: so, --account=PAS3493 becomes the script’s $1, and is not seen by sbatch at all. Therefore, sbatch fails with the same error as above:
sbatch: error: ERROR: Job invalid: Must specify account for job
sbatch: error: Batch job submission failed: Unspecified error
If the account had been specified in some other way, the job would have run and printed the output in option C.





3.2 Where does the script’s output go?

Slurm log files
Above, we saw that when you ran printname.sh “directly” with bash, the script’s output was printed to the screen, whereas when you submitted it as a batch job, only Submitted batch job <job-id> was printed to screen. In the latter case, where did this output go?
It ended up in a file called slurm-<job-id>.out (e.g., slurm-56603792.out; since each job ID is unique to a given job, each file has a different number). We’ll call this type of file a Slurm log file.


Getting this output in log files instead of printed to screen may seem inconvenient. Can you think of any reasons why we may not want batch job output printed to screen, even if it were possible?

There are several reasons, such as:

If you log off after submitting a batch job, any output printed to screen would be lost.
The power of submitting batch jobs is that you can submit many at once — e.g. one per sample, running the same script. If the output from all those scripts ends up on your screen, things become a big mess, and you have no lasting record of what happened.


If you run ls, you should see a Slurm log file for the job you just submitted:
ls
scripts slurm-56603792.out
Let’s take a look at its contents:
# Auto-complete the file name with Tab: you'll have a different job ID!
cat slurm-56603792.out
First name: Jane, last name: Doe
This file contains what the script printed to screen when we ran it with bash — nothing more or less. That includes any error messages: recall from week 4 that besides regular output (“standard output”), commands can also print error messages (“standard error”) to the screen. In a batch job, both end up in the Slurm log file1.






TipThe working directory stays the same



When the scripts in batch jobs are being run, they start in the directory that they were submitted from: that is, the working directory remains the same, and you shouldn’t have to make special adjustments to paths. Additionally, as you’ve seen, Slurm log files will (by default) be created in the dir you submitted the job from.




Cleaning up the Slurm logs
When submitting batch jobs, your working dir can easily become a confusing mess of anonymous-looking Slurm log files. These two strategies help to prevent this:

Changing the Slurm log file name to include a one- or two-word description of the job/script (next lecture).
Cleaning up your Slurm log files, by:

Removing them when no longer needed — as is e.g. appropriate for our current Slurm log file.
Moving them to the same location as other outputs by that script. This is often appropriate after you’ve run a bioinformatics tool, since the Slurm log file may contain some info you’d like to keep. (For example, you can move Slurm log files for jobs that ran FastQC, and produced outputs in results/fastqc, to a dir results/fastqc/logs.)


In this case, we’ll simply remove the Slurm log file, because it has no information that we need to keep:
# Again, auto-complete the file name to include the correct job ID
rm slurm-56603792.out



3.3 Adding sbatch options in scripts
The --account= option is just one of many options you can use when submitting a job, but is the only required one. For all other options, defaults are set, such as the amount of time (1 hour) and the number of cores (1 core).
Instead of adding these options after the sbatch command when submitting the script, you can also add them inside the script. This is a useful alternative because:

You’ll often want to specify several options, which could otherwise lead to very long sbatch commands.
It allows you to store a script’s typical Slurm options as part of the script, so you don’t have to remember them.

These options are added in the script using another type of special comment line (akin to the shebang #!/bin/bash line) that is marked by #SBATCH.






WarningMake sure the #SBATCH lines are at the top of the script (Click to expand)





Just like the shebang line, #SBATCH lines must be located at the top of the script: Slurm stops looking for them as soon as it reaches the first line with a command (comment lines and blank lines before that are fine). Any #SBATCH lines further down are silently ignored: you won’t get an error, but those options won’t be applied either.
Another pitfall is a line that doesn’t start with exactly #SBATCH, like # SBATCH (with a space) or #sbatch — these will similarly be silently ignored.



Let’s add an #SBATCH line to the printname.sh script, such that the first few lines read:


scripts/printname.sh (excerpt)

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=PAS3493
set -euo pipefail

So, the equivalent of adding --account=PAS3493 after sbatch on the command line is a line in your script that reads #SBATCH --account=PAS3493. Now, you can run the sbatch command without options (which failed earlier):
sbatch scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe
Submitted batch job 56603905







Notesbatch option precedence!



If you specify the same sbatch option both on the command line and in the script, the command line option takes precedence, so the one in the script is ignored. This is sensible because it allows you to provide “defaults” inside the script, and change one or more of those when needed “on the go” on the command line.








TipRunning a script with #SBATCH lines in other contexts and on other computers (Click to expand)





Because #SBATCH lines are special comment lines, they will simply be ignored (and not throw any errors) when you run a script with them in other contexts. For example, when you’re running the script with bash instead of sbatch at OSC, or when running it on a computer without Slurm installed. This is convenient and means that these lines do not reduce the portability of your scripts.

title: Slurm batch jobs – part I
text:
4 Monitoring batch jobs
Real batch jobs for your research projects may run for a while. You may also be submitting many jobs at once. Finally, longer-running jobs and those that ask for many cores sometimes remain queued for a while before they start. For these reasons, it’s important to know how you can monitor your batch jobs.

4.1 Checking a job’s status

Batch job behavior
After you submit a job, it may initially be waiting to get resources allocated to it: in other words, the job may be pending. Eventually, and often very quickly, the job will start running. You’ve seen this process with the VS Code Interactive App job as well.
Whereas Interactive App jobs will keep running until they’ve reached the end of the allocated time2, batch jobs will stop as soon as the script has finished. And if the script is still running when the job runs out of its allocated time, it will be killed (stopped) right away.


The squeue command
You can check the status of your batch jobs using the below squeue Slurm command, where:

You specify your username with the -u option (without this, you’d see everyone’s jobs!). In this example, I used the environment variable $USER to get your user name, but you can simply type your username if that’s easier.
The option -l (lowercase L, “long”) will produce the more verbose output shown. Without it, the output will be a bit more cryptic, with abbreviations.

# Or: squeue -u jelmer -l
squeue -u $USER -l
Mon Oct 26 14:21:34 2026
        JOBID PARTITION     NAME     USER    STATE       TIME TIME_LIMI  NODES NODELIST(REASON)
     56603512 condo-osu ondemand   jelmer  RUNNING      36:34   2:00:00      1 p0133
The output always starts with a line with the date & time and a header line with all-caps column names. Then, if there are any jobs in the queue, there will be one line per job. In this case there is only one job in the queue, which is the VS Code Interactive App job.
Across the output columns, the following pieces of information about each job are listed:







Column
Explanation




JOBID
The job ID


PARTITION
The type of queue (usually auto-assigned and not of interest)


NAME
The name of the job (by default the name of the script when submitting a script)


USER
The username of the person who submitted the job


STATE
The job’s state, usually either PENDING or RUNNING (Finished jobs do not appear)


TIME
For how long the job has been running (here in “minutes:seconds” format)


TIME_LIMIT
The amount of time you reserved for the job (here in “hours:minutes:seconds” format)


NODES
The number of nodes reserved for the job


NODELIST(REASON)
– When running: the ID of the node on which it is running.– When pending: why the job is pending






4.2 A sleepy script for practice
We’ll use another short shell script to practice monitoring and managing batch jobs. First create a new file:
touch scripts/sleep.sh
Open the file in the VS Code editor and paste the following into it:


scripts/sleep.sh

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=PAS3493
set -euo pipefail

echo "I will sleep for 30 seconds" > sleep.txt

sleep 30s

echo "I'm awake! Successfully finished script sleep.sh"


First, run the script directly with bash, and notice that you won’t get your prompt back until the script finishes, 30 seconds later:
bash scripts/sleep.sh
I'm awake! Successfully finished script sleep.sh
The other line of text was redirected to sleep.txt:
cat sleep.txt
I will sleep for 30 seconds
Remove the output file before we try this as a batch job:
rm sleep.txt


 Exercise 2: A sleepy batch job
First, predict what would happen if you submit the sleep.sh script above as a batch job using sbatch scripts/sleep.sh:

Which output files will this batch job produce?

Only sleep.txt
Only a Slurm log file
sleep.txt and a Slurm log file
sleep.txt and two Slurm log files: one for output and one for errors



 Click for the solution

(c) The job will produce 2 files:

slurm-<job-id>.out: The Slurm log file, containing output normally printed to screen.
sleep.txt: Containing output that was redirected to this file in the script.


Where will the text “I’m awake! Successfully finished script sleep.sh” end up?

In sleep.txt
In the Slurm log file
On your screen, without being saved to any file



 Click for the solution

(b) “I’m awake! Successfully finished script sleep.sh” is not redirected, so it would normally be printed to screen, and in a batch job, it therefore ends up in the Slurm log file. So, those files will contain the following:

slurm-<job-id>.out: I’m awake! Successfully finished script sleep.sh
sleep.txt: “I will sleep for 30 seconds”


In which directory will the output file(s) appear?

Your home directory
The scripts directory, where sleep.sh is located
The directory from which you submitted the job



 Click for the solution

(c) Both files will end up in your current working directory. Slurm log files always go to the directory from which you submitted the job. Slurm jobs also run from the directory from which you submitted your job, and since we redirected the output simply to sleep.txt, that file was created in our working directory.

Checking your predictions and practicing with squeue:

Test your predictions by submitting the script with sbatch.
Right after submitting, check the queue with squeue -u $USER -l a few times: can you catch the job as PENDING, and then RUNNING?
What happens to it in the squeue output after about 30 seconds?



 Click for the solution

Submit the script:
sbatch scripts/sleep.sh
Submitted batch job 56604062
If you’re quick enough, you may be able to catch the job’s STATE as PENDING before it starts:
squeue -u $USER -l
Mon Oct 26 14:28:26 2026
       JOBID PARTITION     NAME     USER    STATE       TIME TIME_LIMI  NODES NODELIST(REASON)
     56604062 serial-40 sleep.sh   jelmer  PENDING       0:00   1:00:00      1 (None)
     56603512 condo-osu ondemand   jelmer  RUNNING      43:26   2:00:00      1 p0133
But soon enough it should read RUNNING:
squeue -u $USER -l
Mon Oct 26 14:28:39 2026
       JOBID PARTITION     NAME     USER    STATE       TIME TIME_LIMI  NODES NODELIST(REASON)
     56604062 condo-osu sleep.sh   jelmer  RUNNING       0:12   1:00:00      1 p0133
     56603512 condo-osu ondemand   jelmer  RUNNING      43:39   2:00:00      1 p0133
The script finishes after 30 seconds (because of sleep 30s), after which the job immediately disappears from the squeue listing, because only pending and running jobs are shown:
squeue -u $USER -l
Mon Oct 26 14:29:26 2026
       JOBID PARTITION     NAME     USER    STATE       TIME TIME_LIMI  NODES NODELIST(REASON)
     56603512 condo-osu ondemand   jelmer  RUNNING      44:26   2:00:00      1 p0133
Then, check the outputs:
cat sleep.txt
  I will sleep for 30 seconds
cat slurm-56604062.out
I'm awake! Successfully finished script sleep.sh


Now, let’s reason through a variation on this, without actually running it:

Suppose you change the script’s echo line to echo "I will sleep for 30 seconds" > results/sleep.txt, but the results dir doesn’t exist yet. What would happen when you submit the script as a batch job?

The job would succeed, because the results dir would be created automatically.
The job would fail, and the error message would be printed to your screen.
The job would fail, and the error message would be in the Slurm log file.
The job would fail, but you’d only notice because results/sleep.txt is missing: the error message isn’t saved anywhere.



 Click for the solution

(c) The job will fail: echo can’t redirect its output to a file inside a directory that doesn’t exist, so this command will produce an error (something like “No such file or directory”), and because of our strict set -euo pipefail settings, the script will exit immediately at that point. You would find out about this in the Slurm log file slurm-<job-id>.out, which Slurm still creates by default in your submission dir – it will contain the error message.





4.3 Checking a job’s output files

Two types of output
As you saw in Exercise 2, a batch job can produce output in two places. These correspond to an important distinction between two general types of output that scripts, commands, and programs can have:

Output that is printed to screen, both standard output and standard error.

Most shell commands, like echo in sleep.sh, by default print their output to the screen.
Other programs, like you’ve seen with FastQC, only print “logging”-type output (e.g. progress and error messages) to the screen3.

Output that is written to files.

Programs like FastQC write their main results to files.
Shell commands write to files when you redirect their output, like the first echo command in sleep.sh.


Here is what happens to each of these when you submit a script as a batch job instead of running it directly with bash:








Type of output
Run with bash
Submit with sbatch




Printed to screen (stdout/stderr)
Printed to the screen
Written to the Slurm log file


Written to files
Written to those files
Written to the exact same files




In other words, submitting a script as a batch job only changes where “screen output” goes, and not what happens to any output files.
Even if you’ve been monitoring a job with squeue, you should always check both types of output to make sure it ran successfully: the Slurm log file and any output files created by the script.
Let’s keep things tidy and remove the script’s outputs:
rm slurm* sleep.txt







WarningBe careful with deleting Slurm log files



If you delete a Slurm log file for a job that is still running, the file will not be recreated when the job produces more logging output later on. That means that if you accidentally do this and the logging output is of key importance to interpreting other outputs, or making sure it ran successfully, you are better off canceling the job entirely and trying again. 😕





4.4 Canceling jobs
Sometimes, you want to cancel one or more jobs. For example, you may realize you made a mistake in the script or used the wrong input files as arguments. You can cancel jobs that are either pending or running using scancel:

# Cancel a specific job:
scancel 56604061

# Cancel all your running and queued jobs (careful with this!
# This also cancels your VS Code session, since that is a compute job too):
scancel -u $USER



Say you’ve submitted a job, and while it’s still pending, you notice and fix a mistake in the script. Will the job run the fixed script once it starts?

No: when you submit a job, Slurm stores a copy of the script, and that copy is what the job will run. So, after fixing a script, cancel any pending or running jobs that use it, and submit them again.
(But input files are only read when the job runs, so changing those does affect pending jobs.)



 Exercise 3: Cancel a job
Submit the sleep.sh script again, check with squeue that it’s running, and once it has been running for a few seconds, cancel it with scancel. Before checking anything, predict:

Will there be a Slurm log file, and if so, what will be in it?

No: the job was canceled, so no Slurm log file will be created
Yes, and it will contain the “I’m awake!” line
Yes, and it will contain an error message from Slurm



 Click for the solution

(c) There will be a Slurm log file, since the job had already started. It will contain an error message from Slurm like the one below, but not the “I’m awake!” line, because the job was killed during sleep:
slurmstepd: error: *** JOB 56604068 ON p0133 CANCELLED AT 2026-10-26T14:34:02 ***

Will sleep.txt be there?

Yes
No



 Click for the solution

(a) Yes, because the echo line that creates it ran before the sleep command. (If you had canceled the job while it was still pending, neither file would have been created.)


Then, check your predictions, and afterwards, remove the generated files.


 Click for the solution

sbatch scripts/sleep.sh
Submitted batch job 56604068
scancel 56604068
Then, check for the output files and look at the Slurm log file. Finally, clean up:
rm slurm* sleep.txt









NoteAdditional job management commands and options (Click to expand)





Here are some additional job management commands and options:

Use squeue’s -t option to restrict the type of jobs you want to show. For example, to only show running jobs (and not pending jobs):
squeue -u $USER -t RUNNING
You can see more details about any running or recently finished job, including the amount of time it ran for:
scontrol show job <job-id>
JobId=56604070 JobName=sleep.sh
UserId=jelmer(33227) GroupId=PAS0471(3773) MCS_label=N/A
Priority=200005206 Nice=0 Account=PAS3493 QOS=pitzer-default
JobState=RUNNING Reason=None Dependency=(null)
Requeue=1 Restarts=0 BatchFlag=1 Reboot=0 ExitCode=0:0
RunTime=00:02:00 TimeLimit=01:00:00 TimeMin=N/A
SubmitTime=2026-10-26T14:38:44 EligibleTime=2026-10-26T14:38:44
AccrueTime=2026-10-26T14:38:44
StartTime=2026-10-26T14:38:47 EndTime=2026-10-26T15:38:47 Deadline=N/A
SuspendTime=None SecsPreSuspend=0 LastSchedEval=2026-10-26T14:38:47
Partition=serial-40core AllocNode:Sid=pitzer-login01:57954
[...]
Hold and release a pending (queued) job, which could e.g. be useful when you need to update an input file before the job starts running:
scontrol hold <job-id>       # Job won't start running until released
scontrol release <job-id>    # Job is free to start

title: Slurm batch jobs – part I
text:
5 Recap and what’s next
In this lecture, you’ve learned the basics of submitting scripts as Slurm batch jobs with the sbatch command:

How to specify sbatch options on the command line or inside the script
The basic behavior and outputs associated with batch jobs
How to check the job queue, and monitor and cancel your jobs

In the next lecture, you will learn other commonly used sbatch options so you can reserve more time, cores, etc. for your job. You will also see some more practical examples of running batch jobs, update your CLAUDE.md so Claude writes scripts for batch jobs, and zoom out to look at whole workflows.

text:
Footnotes


 Unless you explicitly instruct Slurm to print standard output and standard error to separate files — see this section on the optional self-study page for more.↩︎
Unless you actively “Delete” the job on the OnDemand website.↩︎
 But some programs will by default also print their main results to the screen. This can sometimes be changed with a program’s options, and otherwise, you can always redirect (>) output to a file.↩︎

title: Slurm batch jobs – part II
text:
1 Introduction

1.1 Learning goals
Now that you know the basics of submitting and managing Slurm batch jobs, you will learn:

The most common Slurm/sbatch options, including those used to request:

More time, cores, and memory for jobs
An email notification when jobs e.g. fail or finish

How to run Slurm jobs in practice, including how to submit many jobs at the same time
How to make sure that your jobs succeeded
How to make Claude write scripts for Slurm batch jobs
How to structure a multi-step workflow, and what workflow management systems and nf-core pipelines are



1.2 Getting ready

At https://ondemand.osc.edu, start a VS Code session in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER.
In the terminal, navigate to your week10 dir.

title: Slurm batch jobs – part II
text:
2 Common Slurm/sbatch options
In class, we’ll go through the most commonly used sbatch options using the slides below (open them in a separate tab for a full-screen view).


After that, you’ll think about what happens when a job exceeds its time limit. This section also has a reference table of these and some additional options, and a few more notes on cores, memory, and Slurm log files.

2.1 Exceed the time limit

 Exercise 2: Exceed the time limit
Say you modify your scripts/sleep.sh script from the previous lecture so that it reserves only 1 minute (#SBATCH --time=1), but sleeps for 100 seconds, and then you submit it.
How will the outcome differ from the job you canceled in the previous lecture’s Exercise 3?

If you want to see this for yourself, try it after class, and remove the generated files afterwards.



2.2 sbatch options overview
Here are the main options from the slides:









Resource/use
long option example
short option
default




Project to be billed
--account=PAS3493
-A
N/A


Time limit
--time=4:00:00
-t
1:00:00


Nr of cores
--cpus-per-task=1
-c
1


Memory limit per node
--mem=20G
—
4G per core


Log output file
--output=slurm-fastqc-%j.out
-o
slurm-%j.out


Get email when job fails/ ends or fails
--mail-type=FAIL  --mail-type=END,FAIL
—
(none)




And some additional ones:







Resource/use
long option example




Put error output (stderr) into a separate file
--error=slurm-fastqc-%j.err


Job name (will e.g. be displayed in squeue output)
--job-name=fastqc


Partition (=queue type)
--partition=longserial  --partition=hugemem


Only allow job to begin after a specific time
--begin=2026-10-29T12:00:00


Only allow job to begin after another job has successfully finished
--dependency=afterok:123456


Nr of nodes
--nodes=1


Nr of “tasks” (processes)
--ntasks=1


Nr of tasks per node
--ntasks-per-node=1



For more about --error, --partition, and email warnings before a job hits its time limit, see the optional self-study page on Slurm.






NoteWhat about nodes and tasks? (Click to expand)





You may wonder why the option is --cpus-per-task rather than just --cpus. Slurm can also reserve multiple nodes (--nodes) and multiple tasks, i.e. independent processes (--ntasks). Both default to 1, which is almost always what you want in bioinformatics: for example, multiple nodes are only useful for programs parallelized with “MPI”, which is rare. With 1 node and 1 task, --cpus-per-task simply sets the number of cores.
You may also see --ntasks=n being used for multi-threading, including in OSC’s documentation: in practice, that also gives you n cores that a program can use. (Yes, this is confusing!)









WarningIt is not always clear what happened when your job ran out of memory (Click to expand)





Whereas you get a very clear Slurm error message when you hit the time limit (as seen in Exercise 3), hitting the memory limit can result in a variety of errors.
But look for keywords such as “Killed”, “Out of Memory” / “OOM”, and “Core Dumped”, as well as actual “dumped cores” in your working dir (large files with names like core.<number>, which can be deleted).
If you see these or otherwise suspect that your job ran out of memory, resubmit it with an increased requested amount of memory. To check, you can also use seff to see a finished job’s peak memory use, or sacct, which lists jobs that ran out of memory as OUT_OF_MEMORY (see the optional self-study page).

title: Slurm batch jobs – part II
text:
3 Batch job examples with FastQC
In week 7, we used a for loop to run FastQC for every FASTQ file, one after the other. This ran quickly, but keep in mind that our practice FASTQ files are only 5% of their original sizes. Additionally, other bioinformatics programs may take much longer, even for small files. To speed things up, and not block the terminal while programs are running, we will submit a batch job for each sample/file, so that many jobs can run simultaneously1.
So, let’s practice with submitting a batch job for each FastQC run. We’ll first submit a job for a single file, and then loop over all files to submit many jobs. You should have the FastQC script in scripts/fastqc.sh.

3.1 Modify the script for usage with Slurm
Here, you’ll add Slurm options to the script with #SBATCH lines, and consider whether FastQC should use multiple cores. When you have multiple cores at your disposal in a batch job, you should almost always explicitly tell the program how many cores it can use. Some programs default to using 1 core while others try to auto-detect the number of cores, but any auto-detection tends to be inappropriate at OSC2.

 Exercise 3: Add Slurm options to the FastQC script

Add #SBATCH lines to the top of scripts/fastqc.sh, so that:

The OSC project PAS3493 will be billed
You’ll get an email only if the job fails
The Slurm log file will be named slurm-fastqc-<job-id>.out


Should you also reserve multiple cores for these FastQC batch jobs? Here is the description of FastQC’s option for multi-threading, from its help info:
-t --threads    Specifies the number of files which can be processed
                simultaneously.  Each thread will be allocated 250MB of
                memory so you shouldn't run more threads than your
                available memory will cope with, and not more than
                6 threads on a 32 bit machine
Given that each of our batch jobs will process a single FASTQ file, would, say, 4 cores and --threads 4 make each job faster?





3.2 A single test batch job

Submit the batch job
Now, you’re ready to submit the script. Let’s test it for one sample first:
sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc
Submitted batch job 37615710


Monitor the batch job
Next, monitor your job by checking its status in the Slurm queue:
squeue -u $USER -l
Wed Oct 28 14:31:48 2026
             JOBID PARTITION     NAME     USER    STATE       TIME TIME_LIMI  NODES NODELIST(REASON)
          37615710   cpu-exp fastqc.s   jelmer  RUNNING       0:01   1:00:00      1 p0510
After a while:

You will know that your job has stopped running (either due to failure or because it finished successfully) when it is no longer listed in the squeue output.
If you additionally didn’t receive an email from Slurm, this suggests the job succeeded — job failure should have triggered an email due to the #SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL line.



Check the output files
Even if you’ve inferred that your job succeeded from the abovementioned clues, don’t forget to look at the output files to confirm this:

Slurm log file: The combination of having strict bash set settings and the “Successfully finished” echo line at the end of the script means that if you see that line printed, the script encountered no errors. Nevertheless, you should also look at the rest of this file, because a program’s “logging statements” may have useful information, including output summaries but also warnings.
The program’s main output files: As discussed, most bioinformatics tools don’t just print “logging” information that ends up in the Slurm log file, but will also have output files (in the case of FastQC, an HTML and a Zip file). Therefore, always check the output dir for the presence of such output files.

Check that the Slurm log file ends with the “marker” line that indicates a successful run:
# (You can also Tab-complete your filename instead)
tail slurm-fastqc*.out
Approx 90% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 95% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 100% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Analysis complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz

Used FastQC version:
INFO:    Using cached SIF image
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
FastQC v0.12.1

Successfully finished script fastqc.sh
Wed Oct 28 02:31:51 PM EDT 2026
(With a real analysis, you’d also want to read through the whole file, e.g. with less.)






TipOptional: hide Apptainer’s INFO messages in your Slurm log files (Click to expand)





When you run a program with apptainer exec, Apptainer prints some messages of its own, like “INFO: gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs”. These are harmless, but clutter your Slurm log files. To hide them, add the --quiet option right after apptainer (warnings and errors will still be shown):


scripts/fastqc.sh (excerpt)

apptainer --quiet exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --outdir "$outdir" "$fastq"





Finally, check for the presence of the main FastQC output files:
ls -lh results/fastqc
total 1.1M
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 718K Oct 28 14:31 S63_R1_fastqc.html
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 364K Oct 28 14:31 S63_R1_fastqc.zip
It can also be a good idea to pay attention to the file sizes of outputs, as shown by ls -lh. Especially if you’re not going to open the output files right away, this can be yet another clue as to whether the program succeeded. When they fail, some programs produce empty or extremely small output files — their presence should always be a red flag.


Clean up
Because this was a test-run, and you will now run a loop to analyze each sample, let’s remove the outputs:
rm -r results/fastqc slurm-fastqc*


 Self-study exercise 1: Trigger a job failure email

Before trying it, predict what will happen if you submit scripts/fastqc.sh as a batch job without any arguments:

Will the sbatch command itself give you an error?
What error message will end up in the Slurm log file?
Will a results/fastqc dir be created?



 Click for the solution


No: sbatch doesn’t look at your script’s arguments, so it will simply print Submitted batch job <job-id>. The error only happens later, when the script runs inside the job.
Because of set -u, the script will stop at the line fastq="$1", and the Slurm log file will contain an error like /var/spool/slurmd/job37615711/slurm_script: line 14: $1: unbound variable. (Slurm runs a copy of your script, which explains that odd path, and the line number depends on how many #SBATCH lines your script has.)
No: the script exits before it gets to the mkdir -p line.


Submit the script without arguments, and check your predictions. Then, wait for the failure email to arrive. (If it doesn’t arrive within a few minutes, check the queue to make sure your job isn’t still pending.)
Optional: if you prefer, set a “Rule” in Outlook so the Slurm emails will not go to your Inbox but to a specific folder for such emails.




3.3 Submit a job for each file
Next, we’ll loop over all FASTQ files to submit a job for each file. Though before you do so, let’s do a “mock-run”, just like you did in GA4 — if you preface the command with echo, the command will just be printed instead of executed. That can be really helpful with loops, e.g. to make sure you are looping over the files you want:
for fastq_file in ../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz; do
    echo sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh "$fastq_file" results/fastqc
done
sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc
sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz results/fastqc
sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc
sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R2.fastq.gz results/fastqc
sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S65_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc
sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S65_R2.fastq.gz results/fastqc
# [...output truncated...]
That looked as expected, so now you can actually submit the batch jobs:
for fastq_file in ../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz; do

Take a close look at (at least) one Slurm log file:
less slurm-fastqc-*
# [output not shown]






Tip“Cycle” through files with less



When you pass multiple files to less, like in the command above, it will only open one file at a time, but you can “cycle” through the files: as less itself suggests at the bottom of the screen, successively press : then n to go to the next file.


Check the last few lines of all of them:
tail slurm-fastqc-*

With 44 files, it’s easy to miss a failed job when scrolling through this output. Instead, you can use grep -c, which prints a count for each file when you give it multiple files. Any file with a count of 0 belongs to a job that didn’t finish successfully:
grep -c "Successfully finished" slurm-fastqc-*.out
slurm-fastqc-37615718.out:1
slurm-fastqc-37615719.out:1
# [...output truncated...]
Check for the presence of the FastQC output files:
ls -lh results/fastqc
total 48M
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 718K Oct 28 14:42 S63_R1_fastqc.html
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 364K Oct 28 14:42 S63_R1_fastqc.zip
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 712K Oct 28 14:42 S63_R2_fastqc.html
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 359K Oct 28 14:42 S63_R2_fastqc.zip
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 714K Oct 28 14:42 S64_R1_fastqc.html
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 366K Oct 28 14:42 S64_R1_fastqc.zip
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 709K Oct 28 14:42 S64_R2_fastqc.html

-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 713K Oct 28 14:42 S65_R1_fastqc.html
# [...output truncated...]
And check that there is an HTML file for each of the 44 FASTQ files:
ls results/fastqc/*html | wc -l
44

If everything looks good, and you are convinced that all jobs have finished successfully, all that is left is to clean up the Slurm log files. In this case, it is useful to keep these files around somewhere, as they contain information about our runs (when, which files, what version, etc.). But we want to move them out of our working dir. It often makes sense to store them in a subdir of the program’s outdir, e.g.:
mkdir results/fastqc/logs
mv slurm-fastqc-* results/fastqc/logs/
To avoid moving log files by hand, you can also make your script put a copy of its Slurm log file in the output dir: see this section of the optional self-study page on Slurm.


3.4 Recap: Making sure your jobs ran successfully
To recap, here is an overview of basic strategies to monitor your batch jobs:

To see whether your job(s) have started, check the queue (with squeue) and/or check for Slurm log files (with ls).
Once the jobs are no longer listed in the queue, they will have finished: either successfully or because of an error.
When you’ve submitted many jobs that run the same script for different samples/files:

For at least one of the jobs, carefully read the full Slurm log file, and check other output files.
Check that no jobs have failed: via email when using --mail-type=FAIL, and/or by checking each log for messages like “Successfully finished script” (run grep -c on all logs at once).
Check that you have the expected number of output files (run ls | wc -l) and that no files have size zero (run ls -lh).








TipJob monitoring tip: See output added to the Slurm log file in real time (Click to expand)





Text will be added to the Slurm log file in real time as the running script (or the program run by the script) outputs it. However, the output printed by commands like cat and less is static and not updated in real-time.
Therefore, if you find yourself opening/printing the contents of the Slurm log file again and again to keep track of the job’s progress, then instead use tail -f, which will “follow” the file and will print new text as it’s added to the Slurm log file:
# See the last lines of the file, with new contents added in real time
tail -f slurm-fastqc-37615717.out
To exit the tail -f livestream, press Ctrl+C.

title: Slurm batch jobs – part II
text:
4 Update your CLAUDE.md
GenAI can help with Slurm in many ways: writing #SBATCH lines, writing loops to submit many jobs, and especially figuring out why a job failed from its Slurm log file.
The CLAUDE.md you made in week 9 tells Claude that you haven’t learned about batch jobs, and should therefore run programs with a single core. Copy it into your week10 dir:
cp ../week09/CLAUDE.md .


 Help! I don’t have the CLAUDE.md file

Create a new file CLAUDE.md in your week10 dir, and copy the following into it:


CLAUDE.md

# Practice RNA-Seq project

Practice project for the course PLNTPTH 5006, using RNA-Seq data from Garrigós et al.
(2025) on Culex pipiens mosquitoes infected with two avian Plasmodium species.

## Data

- FASTQ files are in `../garrigos/fastq`: paired-end, ~75-bp Illumina reads for
  22 samples, subsampled to 500,000 reads per file
- Sample metadata is in `../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv`
- Never modify, move, or delete anything in `../garrigos`

## Project structure

- `scripts/`: scripts
- `results/`: all output, in a separate subdir for each step (e.g. `results/fastqc`)

## Computing infrastructure

- We work at the Ohio Supercomputer Center (OSC)
- I haven't yet learned how to submit batch jobs, so don't propose to use these
  (and therefore run programs with a single core/thread)

## Shell script conventions

- Start scripts with `#!/bin/bash` and `set -euo pipefail`
- Below that, add a comment block with the script's purpose and a usage line
  (e.g. `# Usage: bash scripts/fastqc.sh <FASTQ file> <output dir>`)
- Copy arguments to descriptively named, lowercase variables (e.g. `fastq="$1"`);
  use uppercase only for constants (e.g. `CONTAINER=...`)
- At the start, report the script name, the date, and the inputs;
  at the end, report the program version, a success message, and the date
- Create output dirs with `mkdir -p` before writing to them
- Strike a balance between script functionality and robustness vs. simplicity and
  readability: I am a shell beginner
- In script comments, briefly explain any non-obvious commands, options, and constructs
- Programs that aren't available in the system path should be run with Apptainer
  containers from Seqera Containers (`oras://` URLs),
  not with `module load` or by installing them

## AI diary

- After completing a task, add an entry at the bottom of `doc/ai/ai-diary.md`
  with the date, what I asked for, which files you created or changed,
  and any key findings and decisions (including alternatives that were rejected)
- Keep entries short


Then, adjust the “Computing infrastructure” section to make Claude write scripts that follow this week’s conventions, so it now reads:


CLAUDE.md (excerpt)

## Computing infrastructure

- We work at the Ohio Supercomputer Center (OSC)
- We submit shell scripts as Slurm batch jobs with `sbatch`
- Put `#SBATCH` lines directly below the shebang line, with at least:
  `--account=PAS3493`, `--output=slurm-<program>-%j.out`, and `--mail-type=FAIL`
- If a program can use multiple cores, request them with `--cpus-per-task`,
  and set the program's cores/threads option to the same number
- In the usage line of a script, use `sbatch` instead of `bash`
- Don't submit jobs yourself: show me the `sbatch` command instead

title: Slurm batch jobs – part II
text:
5 Zooming out: workflows

5.1 Multi-step workflows
In a typical omics project (and likely in your final project for this course), you need to run multiple consecutive steps to process and analyze your data: you have a “workflow”. So far, we have focused on running individual steps, like FastQC. How do you organize and run your workflow as a whole?
Recall this RNA-seq workflow, going from raw reads to gene counts:





As discussed in week 2, it is a good idea to keep separate Markdown files for:

A “lab notebook” with chronological entries of everything you did, including mishaps and dead ends.
A “protocol” with the final code in order of execution, needed to rerun your project’s entire computational work.



5.2 A protocol example
Here is a (hypothetical) protocol for the workflow above3. Each step runs a single-step script that takes in- and output files as arguments, and is submitted as one or more batch jobs:


protocol.md

# RNA-seq analysis of _Culex pipiens_

- Author: Jane Doe
- Date: 2026-10-28
- This was run at the Ohio Supercomputer Center (OSC)

## Set up: Set the input file paths

```bash
fastq_dir=data/fastq
ref_assembly=data/ref/assembly.fna
ref_transcripts=data/ref/transcripts.fna
```

## Step 1: Read QC with FastQC

`fastqc.sh` runs FastQC on 1 FASTQ file,
and takes 2 arguments: the FASTQ file and the output dir.

```bash
for fastq in "$fastq_dir"/*fastq.gz; do
    sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh "$fastq" results/fastqc
done
```

## Step 2: FastQC summary with MultiQC

`multiqc.sh` runs MultiQC once for all FastQC outputs,
and takes 2 arguments: the input dir (the FastQC output dir) and the output dir.

```bash
sbatch scripts/multiqc.sh results/fastqc results/multiqc
```

## Step 3: Read trimming with TrimGalore

`trimgalore.sh` runs TrimGalore on the paired-end FASTQ files of 1 sample,
and gives the output files the same names as the input files.
It takes 3 arguments: the R1 FASTQ file, the R2 FASTQ file, and the output dir.

```bash
for fastq_r1 in "$fastq_dir"/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    fastq_r2=${fastq_r1/_R1/_R2}
    sbatch scripts/trimgalore.sh "$fastq_r1" "$fastq_r2" results/trimgalore
done
```

## Step 4: Alignment to a reference genome with STAR

`star.sh` aligns the trimmed reads of 1 sample to the reference genome,
and takes 4 arguments: the trimmed R1 and R2 FASTQ files,
the reference genome FASTA file, and the output dir.

```bash
for fastq_r1 in results/trimgalore/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    fastq_r2=${fastq_r1/_R1/_R2}
    sbatch scripts/star.sh "$fastq_r1" "$fastq_r2" "$ref_assembly" results/star
done
```

## Step 5: Gene-level counting with Salmon

`salmon.sh` counts the reads per gene for 1 sample,
and takes 3 arguments: the BAM file from STAR, the reference transcript FASTA file,
and the output dir.

```bash
for bam in results/star/*bam; do
    sbatch scripts/salmon.sh "$bam" "$ref_transcripts" results/salmon
done
```

Structuring your workflow like this makes it relatively straightforward to rerun everything (e.g. with different samples or settings), or to reuse it in another project. And the protocol documents all steps that were taken.
However, you cannot run all of this code at once:


Why can’t all the code be run at once?

The answer will be added after class.




Which steps can be run simultaneously?

The answer will be added after class.




5.3 How about automation?
There are two main ways to automate such a workflow further:

With more advanced Bash and Slurm code, e.g. by combining multiple steps into one script, or by using Slurm “job dependencies” so that jobs only start once the jobs they depend on have finished successfully4. However, the added complexity of such scripts often doesn’t pay off in the time you save (see the optional Slurm self-study page for some examples).
With a “workflow management system”, which provides a way to formally describe and execute pipelines. The two most commonly used ones in bioinformatics are Nextflow  (Di Tommaso et al. 2017) and Snakemake  (Mölder et al. 2025). These can e.g. automatically submit Slurm jobs, rerun only the steps affected by changes or failures, and run the same pipeline on different computers and datasets. Their main disadvantage is a somewhat steep learning curve.

My recommendation is therefore to either:

Accept that your workflow isn’t fully automated and use a Markdown protocol like the one above
Go all-in and use a workflow management system (specifically, Nextflow). This has become a lot more accessible with genAI, and is an excellent use case for genAI, because you can check its work: if you already have a working protocol, you can run the genAI-written pipeline and compare its outputs to those of your protocol.



5.4 Pre-existing pipelines
Also keep in mind that you don’t always have to build your own pipeline. Many publicly available pipelines exist, and Nextflow has by far the best ecosystem of these: the “nf-core” initiative  (Ewels et al. 2020) curates over 150 best-practice, flexible, and well-documented Nextflow pipelines, developed over years by many experts in the field. This saves you from having to figure out which of the many available tools and settings to use.
Next week, we’ll run the most widely used nf-core pipeline, the rnaseq pipeline .

6 Recap and what’s next
In this lecture, you’ve learned:

The most common sbatch options, to request time, cores, and memory, to name your Slurm log files, and to get emails when jobs fail
How to submit a batch job for each file with a loop
How to check that your batch jobs ran successfully
How to make Claude write scripts for Slurm batch jobs
How to structure a multi-step workflow with a Markdown protocol, and what workflow management systems and nf-core pipelines are

In this week’s exercises, you will put all of this into practice with your TrimGalore script from GA4. Next week, you’ll run an nf-core pipeline.
